topicos.titulo: Word stress: the syllable in charge
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: Every Russian word with two or more syllables has one stronger syllable. It is longer, louder and clearer. This is called word stress. STEP 2: In books, stress is shown as a small mark over the strong vowel. In «мама» (MAH-mah), the strength is on the first «ма». Say it slowly: MAH-mah, with the force on «MAH». STEP 3: In «она» (ah-NAH), the strength is on the last syllable. Say: ah-NAH, with the force on «NAH». Notice that the place of the stress changes from one word to another. STEP 4: One-syllable words, like «как» (kahk) and «кто» (kto), are strong all the way through. There is nothing to choose. STEP 5: Russian stress has no fixed place and is almost never written. So whenever you learn a new word, listen to the audio and remember where the stress is. It decides how the vowels sound, and you will see that in session 3.
topicos.comparacao: in English, stress can change a word too: «REcord» (a noun) and «reCORD» (a verb), «PERmit» and «perMIT». Russian works the same way, except that the stress is almost never written.

exemplos.pt: mom: the stress is on the first «ма»
this is: the stress is on «э»
cat: one syllable only, strong all the way through

erros.motivo: In English, many words start with the strong syllable, so it is easy to put the stress first out of habit. In «она́» the strength falls on the last syllable: ah-NAH.

topicos.titulo: Unstressed vowels: «о» sounds like «а» and «е» sounds like «и»
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: A stressed vowel is clear and long. An unstressed vowel is weak and short, and it changes its sound. This is called vowel reduction. STEP 2: Unstressed «о» sounds like «а». In «она» (ah-NAH), the first letter is «о», but you say «ah». In «Москва» (mahsk-VAH), you say «mah», not «moh». STEP 3: Stressed «о» stays «о». In «кот» (koht) and in «метро» (mee-TROH), the «о» carries the stress and sounds like «о». STEP 4: Unstressed «е» sounds almost like «и», a quick «ee». In «метро», the first syllable sounds like «mee». In «сестра» (sees-TRAH), it sounds like «sees». In «ресторан» (rees-tah-RAHN), it sounds like «rees». STEP 5: The respelling next to each word, in this course, already shows the real pronunciation. When it differs from the spelling, trust the respelling and the audio.
topicos.comparacao: you already do this in English without noticing: the unstressed «a» in «banana» or «about» turns into a weak «uh». In Russian the same happens to the «о» and the «е» that are far from the stress.

exemplos.pt: metro: the «е» sounds like «и», read mee-TROH

erros.motivo: Unstressed, the «е» sounds like «и» and the stress falls on «ро»: mee-TROH.

tabela.what_happens: «е» sounds like «и» and the middle «о» sounds like «а»

topicos.titulo: Voiced and voiceless consonants: the end of the word changes
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: A voiced consonant is one where your throat vibrates. Put a hand on your throat and say «v»: you feel it vibrate. Now say «f»: it does not vibrate. «f» is the voiceless partner of «v». STEP 2: Russian has pairs like this: «в» and «ф», «б» and «п», «д» and «т», «г» and «к», «з» and «с», «ж» and «ш». The first of each pair is the voiced one. Today you already know the voiced «в» and the voiceless «к», «т» and «с». The others come in the next lesson. STEP 3: The end-of-word rule: at the end of a word, a voiced consonant loses its vibration and becomes its voiceless partner. That is why «Романов» (rah-MAH-nahf) ends with an «f» sound, although it is written with «в». STEP 4: The neighbour rule: a voiced consonant also becomes voiceless before a voiceless one. In «вкус» (fkoos), which means «taste», the «в» sounds like «f» because it comes before «к». STEP 5: The spelling does not change, only the sound. Always write the word the way it is spelled, and speak the way the audio speaks.
topicos.comparacao: in English the difference between «v» and «f» changes the word: «van» and «fan». It does in Russian too. But at the end of a word that difference disappears and only the voiceless sound is pronounced.

exemplos.pt: surname: read rah-MAH-nahf, with an «f» at the end

erros.motivo: The final «в» loses its vibration: rah-MAH-nahf.

tabela.why: «в» at the end of a word sounds like «ф»
«в» at the end of a word sounds like «ф»

topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: In English you need the verb «to be»: «this is the mother». In Russian, in the present tense, that verb does not appear. STEP 2: To point something out, use «это» (EH-tah), which means «this» or «this is». Then say just the name of the thing: «Это мама» (EH-tah MAH-mah), literally «this mom». STEP 3: With «он» (ohn) and «она» (ah-NAH) it is the same: «Он Антон» (ohn ahn-TOHN), «Она мама» (ah-NAH MAH-mah). There is no word between the subject and the rest. STEP 4: To negate, put «не» (nyeh) before the word: «Это не торт» (EH-tah nyeh tort), this is not a cake. The word «нет» is kept for the short answer: «Нет». STEP 5: To ask a question, keep the same sentence and raise your voice on the word you are asking about: «Это торт?». The word order does not change. STEP 6: There is a word «есть» (yest), which the dictionary translates as «to be». In everyday speech it does not go in these sentences. Do not say «Это есть мама».
topicos.comparacao: in English «She is the mother» has four words, and «is» is required. In Russian «Она мама» is enough, two words. The verb «to be» in the present simply does not exist.

erros.motivo: In the present tense «есть» is not used in place of «is». The sentence has only «Это» and the name.
Inside a sentence, the negation is «не» and it comes before the word. «нет» is the «no» of the short answer.

topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: In English you say «you» to almost everybody. In Russian there are two forms, and choosing the right one shows respect. STEP 2: Use «ты» (tih) with friends, family, young colleagues and children. With «ты», say «Привет!» (pree-VYET) and «Пока!» (pah-KAH). STEP 3: Use «вы» (vih) with strangers, bosses, teachers, older people, and in shops and offices. With «вы», say «Здравствуйте!» (ZDRAH-stvooy-tyeh) and «До свидания!» (dah svee-DAH-nee-yah). Tip: the first «в» in «Здравствуйте» is not pronounced. STEP 4: «вы» is also the plural: if you speak to two people, even friends, you say «вы». STEP 5: When in doubt, use «вы». Nobody is offended by too much respect, and the other person can suggest «ты». STEP 6: Bosses and older people are usually addressed by first name and patronymic, the father's name: «Ирина Петровна» (ee-REE-nah pee-TROV-nah).
topicos.comparacao: English has something similar: «Hey» for a friend and «Sir» or «Madam» for someone who deserves respect. The difference is that, in Russian, the choice is mandatory in every sentence and it changes the greeting.

exemplos.pt: Hello! For a stranger, the boss, the teacher.
What is your name? For a friend.

erros.motivo: «Привет» is intimate. With first name and patronymic, the greeting is «Здравствуйте».
To the boss or to a stranger, ask with «вас», the formal form.
With a close friend, «Здравствуйте» sounds distant.

tabela.situation: Two or more people, even friends

topicos.titulo: How to say your name: «Меня зовут…»
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: To say your name, Russian literally says «me they call…». The ready-made sentence is «Меня зовут Лена» (mee-NYAH zah-VOOT LYEH-nah): «меня» is «me», «зовут» is «they call». Put your own name in place of «Лена». STEP 2: To ask a friend, say «Как тебя зовут?» (kahk tee-BYAH zah-VOOT). To ask someone who deserves respect, say «Как вас зовут?» (kahk vahs zah-VOOT). STEP 3: Notice: there is no word for «my», «is» or «am». The sentence is short and the name comes last, just as it is. STEP 4: After the name, the polite reply is «Очень приятно» (OH-cheen pree-YAHT-nah), «nice to meet you». The other person answers «Мне тоже» (mnyeh TOH-zheh), «me too». STEP 5: For now, learn «меня», «тебя» and «вас» as ready-made blocks. In lesson 14 you will see where these forms come from.
topicos.comparacao: in English you say «my name is» or «I am called». In Russian nobody says «I» or «my»: the sentence uses «me they call», and the name comes at the end.

exemplos.pt: What is your name? For a friend.

erros.motivo: The sentence does not start with «я». Russian says «меня зовут», «me they call».
The question uses «тебя», not «ты». It is a ready-made form.
To a teacher, a boss or a stranger, use «вас».

tabela.situation: With the boss or a stranger
tabela.question: Как вас зовут?

topicos.titulo: Pronouns and the missing verb «to be»
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: Pronouns are short words, and you have already used three: «я» (yah), I; «ты» (tih), you (informal); and «вы» (vih), you (formal or plural). STEP 2: The others are «он» (ohn), he; «она» (ah-NAH), she; «оно» (ah-NOH), it, for neuter things; «мы» (mih), we; and «они» (ah-NEE), they. STEP 3: Russian has no verb «to be» in the present tense. To say «I am a student», say only «Я студент» (yah stoo-DYENT). Literally: «I student». STEP 4: This applies to all pronouns: «Он студент», «Она студентка», «Мы тут», «Они там». No verb in the middle. STEP 5: In writing, between two nouns, a dash is sometimes put in place of the «is»: «Антон — студент». When speaking, make a small pause where the dash is. STEP 6: A man says «студент» and a woman says «студентка». With «Я», the next word shows the gender of the speaker.
topicos.comparacao: in English the verb changes with the person: «I am», «he is», «we are». In Russian, in the present tense, nothing changes and nothing appears: only the pronoun and the rest of the sentence.

exemplos.pt: I am a student. A man is speaking.
Are you a student? To a friend.

erros.motivo: In the present tense «есть» is not used in place of «is». The pronoun and the word are enough.
For a woman, the word changes: «студентка».

topicos.titulo: The gender of nouns: masculine, feminine and neuter
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: Every Russian noun has a gender: masculine, feminine or neuter. You find the gender by looking at the last letter. STEP 2: Ends in a consonant, or in «й»: masculine. Examples: «брат» (braht), «дом» (dohm), «город» (GOH-raht) and «музей» (moo-ZEY). STEP 3: Ends in «а»: feminine. Examples: «мама» (MAH-mah), «сестра» (sees-TRAH), «школа» (SHKOH-lah) and «жена» (zhee-NAH). STEP 4: Ends in «о»: neuter. Examples: «кино» (kee-NOH), «метро» (mee-TROH) and «фото» (FOH-tah). STEP 5: Careful: in English only people and some animals have a gender (he and she), while things are «it». In Russian every noun has one, so a thing can be «he» or «she»: «брат» is «он», «сестра» is «она», and «кино» is «оно». «Игра», game, is feminine in Russian. And «папа» is masculine, although it ends in «а», because he is a man. STEP 6: The gender chooses the pronoun: masculine is «он», feminine is «она» and neuter is «оно». That is why «брат» is «он», «сестра» is «она» and «кино» is «оно». You will see other endings in lessons 4 and 5.
topicos.comparacao: English has no articles that show gender, so you never had to think about it. Russian has no articles either: the ending of the word is what shows the gender.

exemplos.pt: This is the brother. He is a student.
This is the sister. She is a student.
This is the house. It is over there.
This is the school. It is over there.
This is the cinema. It is over there.
This is the photo. It is here.

erros.motivo: «Папа» ends in «а», but he is a man. That is why it is masculine and the pronoun is «он».
Words ending in «о» are neuter. The pronoun is «оно», not «она».

topicos.titulo: The Cyrillic alphabet: where to start
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: A scene you have lived (or will live). Imagine it. You are in Russia. You come out of the metro and see a big sign, with strange letters that look like a secret code. The sign says: РЕСТОРАН You look at it and think: "That's impossible. It looks Chinese, it looks Greek, it looks... like nothing I know." You take a photo and give up. Now imagine the same scene one hour later. You look at the same sign and read it aloud: Restoran. It is the same word: restaurant. In Russian, restaurant is written ресторан. And the word has been right there in front of you from the start. You just could not read it. This lesson is about that hour. In sixty minutes of careful reading, you will be able to read any Russian sign. You will not understand every word yet, but you will read it. And that is the beginning of everything. STEP 2: The good news: you do not need to memorise 33 things. The Russian alphabet has 33 letters. When you see that number, your brain panics. "Thirty-three! Impossible!" But here is some good news: you do not need to memorise 33 letters. You need to memorise about 15. The other 18 you already know or recognise. How? Because Russian letters fall into four groups: • 1. Letters identical to English (5): A, K, M, O, T. • 2. Letters that look like English ones but have a different sound (7): В, Е, Н, Р, С, У, Х. • 3. New letters with sounds you already know (13): Б, Г, Д, Ё, З, И, Й, Л, П, Ф, Э, Ю, Я. • 4. Truly new letters with new sounds (8): Ж, Ц, Ч, Ш, Щ, Ъ, Ы, Ь. Total: 33 letters. But of the 4 groups, groups 1 and 2 are almost free. Group 3 you learn in an hour. Group 4 is the only one that takes effort. Let's go step by step. STEP 3: Before we start: why the alphabet is called Cyrillic. The Russian alphabet is called Cyrillic (кириллица) because it was created by Saint Cyril, a Greek monk, in the 9th century. He wanted to translate the Bible into the Slavic languages, and for that he needed an alphabet. Since he was Greek, he based the alphabet on Greek, with adaptations. What this means for you: many Russian letters look like Greek letters you have seen in maths, physics or elsewhere: Г (gamma) — looks like a reversed "g" Д (delta) — looks like a "d" with legs Л (lambda) — looks like an "l" with legs П (pi) — looks like a "p" with legs Ф (phi) — looks like an "f" with a circle If you have seen these Greek letters, you are already halfway there.

GROUP 1 — The letters identical to English. Five letters are the same as English in shape and sound. You already know them. You do not have to do anything. Notice: these five letters are identical to English. No trick. No exception. You already know them. Mental exercise: try to read these words using only these five letters: том → tom (volume) кот → koht (cat) мак → mahk (poppy) такт → tahkt (beat) ком → kohm (lump) You are already reading Russian. Without having studied anything. GROUP 2 — The "false friend" letters. Here is the first danger. There are seven letters that look like English letters but sound different. They are the "false friends": they look familiar, but they deceive you. I will give you a mnemonic table. Remember this: the golden rule of Group 2: if a letter looks Latin but is not, be suspicious. Russian borrowed the shape but changed the sound. Mental exercise: read these words with the false friends: вам → vahm (to you) нет → nyet (no) нос → nohs (nose) рука́ → roo-KAH (hand) сон → sohn (sleep, dream) ус → oos (moustache) хор → khohr (choir) You are already reading whole words in Russian.

tabelas.titulo: GROUP 1 — The letters identical to English

"R" (rolled or tapped, like the "tt" in American butter)
"KH" (a rough sound from the throat, like "ch" in Scottish loch)

linhas.FALSE FRIEND: В looks like B but is V
Е looks like E but is YE
Н looks like H but is N
Р looks like P but is R
С looks like C but is S
У looks like Y but is OO
Х looks like X but is KH

topicos.explicacao: GROUP 3 — New letters with sounds you already know. Here is the easy part. Thirteen letters are new in shape, but the sounds are ones you already know (or nearly). You only need to learn to link shape + sound. I will give you tricks for the most important ones: Б looks like "B", and it really is "B". Easy. Г looks like a reversed "G", and it is "G" as in go. Always hard. Д looks like a little house on legs, and it is "D". Ё is Е with two dots. Always stressed, sound "yo". З looks like a "3", and it is "Z" as in zebra. И looks like a reversed "N", and it is "EE". Й is И with an accent mark. A weak "y" sound. Л looks like an "L" with legs, and it is "L". П looks like a Greek "P" (pi), and it is "P". Ф looks like a Greek "F" (phi), and it is "F". Э looks like a mirrored "E", and it is an open "E", as in met. Ю is "Y" + "OO" together: sound "yoo". Я is "Y" + "A" together: sound "yah". Mental exercise: read these words: брат → braht (brother) го́род → GOH-raht (city) дом → dohm (house) ёлка → YOHL-kah (fir tree) зуб → zoop (tooth) игра́ → ee-GRAH (game) мой → moy (mih) лампа → LAHM-pah (lamp) па́па → PAH-pah (dad) футбо́л → foot-BOHL (football) э́то → EH-tah (this is) юг → yook (south) я → yah (I) Notice: you have just read 13 Russian words. Without memorising any list. Without suffering.

tabelas.titulo: GROUP 3 — New letters with sounds you already know

linhas.SOUND (ENGLISH): a weak "y", like the end of boy (semivowel)

topicos.explicacao: GROUP 4 — Truly new letters (and new sounds). Here is the group that takes effort. There are eight letters with a new shape and a new sound. You really have to memorise them. I will explain each one calmly: Ж — like the «s» in «measure» Ж is the «zh» sound, as in «measure», «vision» or the «g» in «genre». It looks like a butterfly or an insect. жена́ → zhee-NAH (wife) журна́л → zhoor-NAHL (magazine) жизнь → zheezn (life) Ц — like the «ts» in «cats» Ц is the «ts» sound at the end of «cats» or «pizza». It looks like a «U» with a little tail. цена́ → tsee-NAH (price) центр → tsentr (center) коне́ц → kah-NYEHTS (end) Ч — like the «ch» in «chat» Ч is the «ch» sound of «chair». It looks like a «4». час → chahs (hour) чай → chy (tea) челове́к → chee-lah-VYEK (person) Ш — like the «sh» in «shop» Ш is the «sh» sound of «ship» and «shop». It looks like three vertical strokes joined at the bottom. шко́ла → SHKOH-lah (school) шапка → SHAHP-kah (hat) шум → shoom (noise) Щ — a longer, softer «sh-ch» Щ is a longer «sh» followed by a light «ch», as in «fresh cheese» said quickly. It looks like a «Ш» with a little tail. щи → shchee (cabbage soup) борщ → borshch (beet soup) това́рищ → tah-VAH-reeshch (comrade) Ъ — the hard sign (no sound) Ъ is a sign that has no sound of its own. It separates a consonant from a vowel, keeping the consonant hard. It appears in few words. объе́кт → ab-YEKT (object) объясни́ть → ab-yas-NEET (to explain) съесть → syest (to eat up) Ы — the throaty «ee» Ы is the hardest sound for English speakers. Say «ih» as in «bit», then pull your tongue back and down while keeping your lips relaxed and spread, not rounded. мы → mih (we) вы → vih (you) сын → sihn (son) ры́ба → RIH-bah (fish) Tip: say «ee», then pull your tongue back without moving your lips. The result is roughly «ы». Ь — the soft sign (no sound) Ь is a sign that has no sound of its own. It softens the consonant before it. That is, the consonant that comes before it is pronounced with a very light «y» after it. день → dyen' (day) ночь → noch' (night) мать → maht' (mother) слова́рь → slah-VAR' (dictionary) Tip: imagine you are saying the word and, at the end, you sketch a very light «y». That is it.

tabelas.titulo: GROUP 4 — Truly new letters (and new sounds)

linhas.EXPLANATION: Like the «s» in «measure», a little harder
Like the «ts» at the end of «cats»
Like a longer «sh», with a light «ch»
Hard sign: separates the consonant from the vowel
An «ee» said with the tongue pulled back, lips relaxed
Soft sign: softens the previous consonant

topicos.titulo: The alphabet table and phonetic spelling
topicos.explicacao: The full table of the Russian alphabet. Here is the complete alphabet, in the correct order. Look at the columns: Note: the Cyrillic order is its own; it is inherited from the Greek alphabet. The big insight: the Russian alphabet is PHONETIC. Here is the most important thing in this lesson. Pay attention. In English, the same letter can have many sounds. Take the C: cat → «k» sound, city → «s» sound, church → «ch» sound, ocean → «sh» sound. Take «ough»: though, through, rough, cough, bough — five different sounds. This is a nightmare even for people learning English. But Russian is different. In Russian, each letter almost always has one fixed sound. Learn the letter, learn the sound. Full stop. There are two exceptions (we will see them in the next section), but they are predictable exceptions. Russian is much more phonetic than English. This is one of the reasons Russian is easier for an English speaker than it looks. You do not need to guess the pronunciation: you read it.

topicos.titulo: The two pronunciation rules you need to know now
topicos.explicacao: The two pronunciation rules you need to know now. There are two pronunciation rules that show up from the very beginning. You need to learn them now. Rule 1: Unstressed «О» becomes «А» In Russian, the letter О sounds like «o» only when it is stressed (with the stress mark). When it is unstressed, it sounds like «a». Examples: This is why you will see spellings such as «mahsk-VAH» and «mah-lah-KOH» in books. That is the real pronunciation. Russians do not say «mohsk-VAH», they say «mahsk-VAH». What to do: when you learn a new word, learn it with the stress mark. Without the stress mark, you do not know whether the «o» is «o» or «a». Keep the word with its stress. Rule 2: Voiced consonants at the end become voiceless In Russian, if a word ends in a voiced consonant (Б, В, Г, Д, Ж, З), it is pronounced as the corresponding voiceless consonant (П, Ф, К, Т, Ш, С). Examples: This is why you will see spellings such as «drook» and «GOH-raht». That is the real pronunciation. Russians do not say «droog», they say «drook». What to do: when you learn a word, listen to the pronunciation. With time, your ear takes over.

topicos.explicacao: To say your name in Russian you use «зовут» (they call) + a pronoun in the accusative, the object form (me, you, him, her, us, them). Literally: «me they call…».

topicos.titulo: How to recognise the letters on the street
topicos.explicacao: How to recognise the letters on the street. Here is a mental exercise that changes everything. Imagine you are in Russia and you see a sign. You look at the sign and try to recognise the letters. Let's practise with real signs. Sign 1: РЕСТОРАН Р = R Е = YE С = S Т = T О = O Р = R А = A Н = N Result: RESTORAN = Restaurant. Sign 2: МЕТРО М = M Е = YE Т = T Р = R О = O Result: METRO = Metro. Sign 3: АПТЕКА А = A П = P Т = T Е = YE К = K А = A Result: APTEKA = Pharmacy. Sign 4: БАНК Б = B А = A Н = N К = K Result: BANK = Bank. Sign 5: ОТЕЛЬ О = O Т = T Е = YE Л = L Ь = soft sign Result: OTEL = Hotel. Sign 6: ТЕАТР Т = T Е = YE А = A Т = T Р = R Result: TEATR = Theatre. Notice: you have just read six Russian signs. Without memorising a complicated alphabet. Without suffering. That is what the Russian alphabet does. It is much friendlier than it looks.

topicos.titulo: Hard vowels and soft vowels: the key to the consonants
topicos.explicacao: Hard vowels and soft vowels: the key to the consonants. Here is a concept you need to understand from the start. It will appear in every lesson that follows. Russian vowels come in two families: HARD vowels (5): SOFT vowels (5): Notice: А ↔ Я (a ↔ ya) О ↔ Ё (o ↔ yo) У ↔ Ю (oo ↔ yoo) Э ↔ Е (e ↔ ye) Ы ↔ И (throaty ee ↔ ee) Each hard vowel has a matching soft vowel. This is fundamental because: when a consonant comes before a soft vowel, it is pronounced "softened" (palatalised). When it comes before a hard vowel, it is "hard". Examples: но (noh) → hard "n" нё (nyo) → softened "n" ну (noo) → hard "n" ню (nyoo) → softened "n" For now, you do not need to worry about this. But know that: the soft vowels (Я, Ё, Ю, Е, И) are the "secret" to understanding Russian consonants. Whenever you see one of these letters after a consonant, the consonant is "soft". We will see this in practice in the next section.

Hard vowels and soft vowels: the key to the consonants

topicos.titulo: Voiceless and voiced consonants; cursive handwriting
topicos.explicacao: Voiceless and voiced consonants. In Russian, consonants fall into two groups, forming pairs: How it works: Voiceless consonants are pronounced without vibration of the vocal cords (like "p", "f", "k", "t", "s", "sh"). Voiced consonants are pronounced with vibration of the vocal cords (like "b", "v", "g", "d", "z", "zh"). The rule: when a voiced consonant is at the end of a word, it is pronounced as the matching voiceless one. Examples: This is why "друг" sounds like "drook". The letter Г at the end of the word becomes К. How to write in Russian cursive. An important detail: Russians write in cursive very often. You will see handwritten texts with letters different from the printed ones. Here is a small table of the main differences: For now, focus on the printed letters. When you come across handwritten Russian texts, you will learn cursive little by little.

In everyday speech, do not use «есть» for «is». The sentence is: «Это» + noun.

Every Russian noun has a gender, and the adjective agrees with it. Masculine: ends in a consonant (дом, стол). Feminine: ends in -а or -я (книга, машина). Neuter: ends in -о or -е (окно). The adjective changes with it: новый (m), новая (f), новое (n). Careful: gender belongs to the Russian word, not to the thing: книга (book) is feminine, while окно (window) is neuter. English has nothing like this, so learn each noun together with its ending. You will practise this calmly in lesson 11.

In everyday speech Russian does not use a verb «to have». It uses «У меня есть», literally «by me there is». Swap «меня» for the other persons. Watch out: after «у», the pronouns «он», «она» and «они» gain an «н-»: у него, у неё, у них.

Since there is no «to be» in the present tense, you say «Я врач» (literally «I doctor»). Many job names have no feminine form: «Она врач», «Она инженер». Some do: студент → студентка, учитель → учительница.

topicos.titulo: Saying «not» with «не» and where you are from
topicos.explicacao: Put «не» before the word you are negating: «Я не врач». To say where you are from, use «Я из» + country. The form of the country changes after «из»; for now, learn it as a ready-made phrase.

To say you do NOT have something, use «нет» and the noun changes form (genitive case): «У меня есть сестра» → «У меня нет сестры». Rule of thumb: -а becomes -ы; -я becomes -и; a final consonant gains -а; after г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ you write -и, never -ы. With «нет» you do not use «есть».
Drop the -ть and add the endings -ю, -ешь, -ет, -ем, -ете, -ют. The verb «жить» is a little different (живу, живёшь...), but it uses the same endings.

To say where, use «в» (inside) or «на» (on top of; also at events and some places) and the noun gains -е: дом → в доме. Words in -ия make -ии: в Бразилии, в России. With «работа», «улица» and «урок» use «на»: на работе, на улице, на уроке. «Кафе» does not change: в кафе.
Verbs in -ать follow the pattern of «работать»: -ю, -ешь, -ет, -ем, -ете, -ют.

What you read, hear or love goes into the accusative. Only feminine words in -а and -я change: -а → -у, -я → -ю. Masculine and neuter nouns that are not people or animals do not change. Masculine people and animals use the same form as after «нет» (genitive): Я люблю брата. The verbs «любить», «смотреть» and «говорить» follow a different pattern: люблю, любишь, любит, любим, любите, любят.

topicos.titulo: The noun: no articles, and gender from the last letter
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: First things first: what is a noun? You have heard the word "noun" a thousand times at school, but it matters for what comes next. A noun is a naming word. It names things, people, places, ideas, feelings: house, map, dog, friendship, coffee, Brazil. It is the "who" or "what" of a sentence. If you can point at something and give it a name, that name is a noun. In English you hardly think about it, because you learned the language naturally. But in Russian the noun has one property that decides almost everything that follows: gender. STEP 2: First piece of good news: Russian has no articles. Breathe out. Russian has no «the» and no «a/an». Nothing. Дом can mean "house", "the house" or "a house", and the context decides. You never have to worry about an article. Zero. But that creates a new question. In English you can say "the book" and "a book" and the noun itself needs no gender at all: a book is just "it". In Russian every noun belongs to a gender, and the word itself has to carry that information. So if there is no article to help, who decides the gender? STEP 3: Who decides the gender: the last letter. Straight answer: the last letter of the word. No article, no argument. And here is the second surprise: Russian has three genders, not two. • 1. Masculine, like «он» (he) • 2. Feminine, like «она» (she) • 3. Neuter, like «оно» (it). Neuter is the closest to your English "it", but be careful: in English every thing is "it". In Russian a table is «он» (he), a book is «она» (she), and only some things are «оно». You have probably heard that Russian has a "neuter gender". That is it: a third box where the words that are neither masculine nor feminine end up. The gender is not a guess about meaning. It is a label you read from the ending.

topicos.titulo: Gender from the ending: the table and the three-second rule
topicos.explicacao: The master table: gender from the ending. Here is the rule that solves about 95% of cases. Look at the last letter. Apply the table. Done. Ends in a consonant? Masculine. Ends in -а or -я? Feminine. Ends in -о, -е or -мя? Neuter. Ends in -ь? You need to check a dictionary, and I will explain why in a moment. The three-second protocol. For any new word you meet, do this: • 1. Look at the last letter. • 2. Apply the rule: consonant or -й → masculine; -а or -я → feminine; -о, -е or -мя → neuter; -ь → dictionary. • 3. Write the word down together with its gender. Always. Never memorise a Russian word without its gender. The right flashcard is not "дом = house". It is "дом = house (masculine)". The gender always travels with the word, because, as you will see in the next lesson, the adjective depends on it. Does it sound simple? It is simple. But there are a few traps, and we talk about them next.

topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: TRAP No. 1: the soft sign (-ь). The -ь (called the "soft sign", мягкий знак) is the pebble in every Russian learner's shoe. It has no sound of its own. It is not a vowel and not a consonant. It is a sign that softens the consonant before it, a bit like a seasoning that changes the texture of the sound without adding anything. For gender it is ambiguous: some nouns in -ь are masculine, others feminine. There is no rule and no logic, so you check a dictionary. Look at the table below. How do you know? Only by looking the word up. But don't despair: with time you will hear the gender, because the adjectives that go with the word give the game away. A Russian says большо́й день ("a big day") and больша́я ночь ("a big night"). The ending of the adjective tells you whether the noun is masculine or feminine. That is next lesson's topic. For now, remember: -ь means dictionary. Don't guess. Look it up, and write the gender down with the word. STEP 2: TRAP No. 2: -мя. Words ending in -мя are neuter. Always. And there are few: about ten in the whole language. You do not have to learn them all at once. The two most common are: имя (EE-mya) — name; вре́мя (VRE-mya) — time. The others (знамя, семя, пламя, стремя, племя, темя, бремя, вымя) are rarer, but the rule is the same: -мя = neuter. You have just learned the rule for all of them in one go. That is what a rule is for: it works even for words you have never seen. STEP 3: TRAP No. 3: the celebrity «кофе». Here is the most famous exception in the language. Ко́фе (KO-fee) means coffee. It ends in -е, so by the rule it should be neuter. But it is masculine. Why? History. The word came into Russian as кофий, which was masculine. Over time it shrank to кофе, but the gender stayed: a linguistic fossil. Remember: вку́сный ко́фе (tasty coffee), not «вкусное кофе». (Modern grammars tolerate the neuter in casual speech, but masculine is the classic, recommended form. Use the masculine.)

In English we say «the book» and «a book». Russian has no «the» and no «a» or «an»: the word «книга» can mean «the book» or «a book», and the context decides. That is why you must remember the gender of every noun (masculine, feminine or neuter). Gender controls the adjective, the possessive and the past-tense verb.
topicos.comparacao: the / a / an + noun. In Russian only the noun appears.

exemplos.pt: This is a book / the book.
This is a house / the house.
This is a window / the window.

topicos.titulo: Gender traps 2: masculines in -а/-я, «дитя», two-gender words and loanwords
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: TRAP No. 4: nouns in -а/-я that are masculine. Not every word that ends in -а or -я is feminine. There are exceptions, and they matter because they name male people. па́па (PAH-pa) — dad; де́душка (DYEH-doosh-ka) — grandad; дя́дя (DYAH-dya) — uncle; мужчи́на (moosh-CHEE-na) — man; ю́ноша (YOO-na-sha) — young man; судья́ (soo-DYAH) — judge; ста́роста (STAH-ra-sta) — group leader; Ники́та (nee-KEE-ta) — Nikita (a male name); Илья́ (eel-YAH) — Ilya (a male name); Лёва (LYO-va) — Lyova (short for Lev); Са́ша (SAH-sha) — Sasha (short for Alexander or Alexandra); Же́ня (ZHEH-nya) — Zhenya (short for Evgeny or Evgenia). They all end in -а or -я but are masculine, because they name men. The ending rule works for most words, but for people the meaning wins. This is an exception you will use every day, so memorise it. STEP 2: TRAP No. 5: дитя, the child. Дитя́ (dee-TYAH) means child, in a poetic or old-fashioned sense. It is the only neuter word that names a person; all the other words for people are masculine or feminine. In everyday speech you will say ребёнок (a masculine word) instead. STEP 3: TRAP No. 6: two-gender nouns. Some words can be masculine or feminine, depending on the sex of the person they name: сирота́ (see-ra-TAH) — orphan (boy or girl); у́мница (OOM-nee-tsa) — clever boy or girl; пья́ница (PYAH-nee-tsa) — drunkard; о́бжора (OB-zho-ra) — glutton; бродя́га (bra-DYAH-ga) — tramp. The word does not change; the adjective next to it shows the gender. That is next lesson's topic. STEP 4: TRAP No. 7: loanwords. Foreign words that enter Russian sometimes break the rules. The main patterns: Ending in -и, -у, -ю → usually neuter: такси́ (taxi), меню́ (menu), кенгуру́ (kangaroo), киви́ (kiwi), желе́ (jelly), кафе́ (café; careful: кофе is masculine and кафе is neuter!), метро́ (metro), кино́ (cinema), пальто́ (coat), бюро́ (office). Ending in a consonant but naming a woman → feminine: ле́ди (lady), Мэ́ри (Mary), Ма́ргарет (Margaret). Ending in -о and naming a man → masculine: маэ́стро (maestro), импреса́рио (impresario). Each case is a case. But the most common pattern is: a loanword ending in a vowel other than -а/-я → neuter. Indeclinable place names such as Токио (Tokyo) are neuter too, as are most foreign names of cities and countries that end in a vowel.

topicos.titulo: The big surprise: an English word tells you nothing about Russian gender
topicos.explicacao: This is where the confusion starts for English speakers, and it is rarely explained clearly. In English, things have no gender: a table, a book, a city are all just "it". So you might expect Russian to work the same way, or at least to follow the meaning. It does not. Every Russian noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, and the gender does not follow meaning: a table is «он» (he), a book is «она» (she), a name is «оно» (it). Look at the table. On the left, the English word. In the middle, the Russian word. On the right, the gender and the reason. The lesson in one sentence: the meaning of the word never tells you the gender; only the ending does. Do not try to guess from what the thing is. Look at the last letter. This is not a detail. It is the difference between speaking Russian and speaking English with Russian words. Another language, another logic: the rules belong to it, not to you. (If you also know French, Spanish or German: don't use their genders either. Russian has its own, and it often differs from them.)

linhas.RUSSIAN GENDER: masculine or feminine (it declines like a feminine noun)

topicos.explicacao: Look at the last letter of the noun in the singular. Masculine: ends in a consonant (стол, дом), in -й (музей) or in -ь (день, словарь). Feminine: ends in -а or -я (книга, неделя), or in -ь (ночь, тетрадь). Neuter: ends in -о, -е or -мя (окно, море, имя, время). Step by step: (1) look at the last letter; (2) if it is -ь, check the list or a dictionary; (3) check whether there is a suffix that gives the gender away (-тель, -ость, -ие...). Two cautions: (1) words in -ь can be masculine or feminine and there is no rule, so memorise the gender together with the word; (2) men whose names end in -а or -я are masculine: папа, дедушка, дядя, мужчина.
topicos.comparacao: English has no grammatical gender for things, so this is new: you cannot guess it from the meaning. Russian nearly always shows the gender in the ending, but it does not follow the meaning: книга (book) is feminine, письмо (letter) is neuter, стол (table) is masculine.

topicos.titulo: The English-speaker's earthquake: words whose gender will surprise you
topicos.explicacao: This section is usually missing from grammars, but it is the one you will use most. English has no grammatical gender for things, so your brain has an autopilot that says "thing = it". When you see "book" your brain thinks "it". In Russian that autopilot lets you down, and badly: nearly every thing is secretly he or she, and only some things are really «оно». Here is a list of words that English speakers almost always get wrong on the first try. Learn these and you will save months of confusion. 🔴 Things you think of as "it", but that are FEMININE in Russian (they end in -а/-я). 🔴 Things you think of as "it", but that are MASCULINE in Russian (they end in a consonant). 🔴 Things that are NEUTER in Russian, which the rest of Europe often makes masculine or feminine (so if you also speak another language, be careful). 🔴 Words in -ь, where you cannot tell from the ending alone. 🔴 The meaning trap: some words that look like people or animals follow the ending, not the sex (собака is feminine, even for a male dog). Here are the most common cases. These words show up in beginner texts all the time, and they are the ones that catch learners out. Memorise them.

topicos.explicacao: Masculine: consonant + -ы (стол → столы); -й and -ь become -и (музей → музеи, словарь → словари). Feminine: -а becomes -ы; -я and -ь become -и (книга → книги, неделя → недели, ночь → ночи). Neuter: -о becomes -а and -е becomes -я (окно → окна, море → моря). Spelling rule: after г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ you never write -ы, but -и (книга → книги, ручка → ручки). You have already met irregular ones: друг → друзья, брат → братья, ребёнок → дети, человек → люди.

topicos.titulo: The adjective: the idea and the fixed-stem rule
topicos.explicacao: What is an adjective? The "can you pick it up?" test. Before any table, a simple question: what is an adjective? An adjective is the word that completes a noun. It is the quality, the characteristic, the way a thing is. And there is a foolproof test to spot one. Can you pick "big" up in your hand? No. "New"? No. "Yellow"? No. But you can pick up a big thing, a new house, a yellow car. You pick up the thing, never the quality. A quality that only exists stuck to a noun = an adjective. That goes for new, old, tall, short, yellow, red, pretty, ugly, expensive, cheap, hot, cold, clever, strange. All adjectives; all of them need a noun to exist. And that is why the Russian adjective agrees with the noun. If the noun is masculine, the adjective is masculine. If the noun is feminine, the adjective is feminine. If it is neuter, the adjective is neuter. English adjectives never change ("a new house", "new houses"). Russian adjectives change all the time, and in a clear, systematic way: the ending shows the gender and number. The golden rule: the stem never changes. Here is the information that will set you free. Every Russian adjective is a two-piece LEGO: STEM (untouchable) + ENDING (movable). The stem carries the meaning. The ending carries the grammar. So when the adjective has to change gender (masculine → feminine → neuter), the stem stays put and only the ending moves. Think of English "actor / actress" or "blond / blonde": a small change at the end, same word. Russian does the same all the time, only the endings are "longer", and that is what scares learners. But the logic is identical. Here is the adjective "new" in Russian. The stem НОВ- never changed. Only the ending. Always.

tabelas.titulo: The golden rule: the stem never changes

topicos.titulo: The "scissors" method: never get it wrong again
topicos.explicacao: The "scissors" method: never get it wrong again. Now the method that will be your tool for life. I call it "the scissors": cut the last two letters off the masculine. You have the stem. Paste on the new ending. Done: the adjective has changed gender. It works because the masculine endings -ЫЙ, -ОЙ, -ИЙ have exactly two letters each. A perfect fit. In practice. Adjective: но́вый (new). • 1. Cut the last two letters: но́в (the stem). • 2. Paste the feminine ending: но́в + ая = но́вая. • 3. Paste the neuter ending: но́в + ое = но́вое. • 4. Paste the plural ending: но́в + ые = но́вые. Adjective: большо́й (big). • 1. Cut the last two letters: больш (the stem). • 2. Feminine: больш + а́я = больша́я. • 3. Neuter: больш + о́е = большо́е. • 4. Plural: больш + и́е = больши́е. Adjective: си́ний (blue). • 1. Cut the last two letters: син (the stem). • 2. Feminine: син + яя = си́няя. • 3. Neuter: син + ее = си́нее. • 4. Plural: син + ие = си́ние. Notice it? It is always the same operation: cut two letters, paste a new one. Always. The conclusion that is worth the whole lesson: if you know ONE adjective form, the masculine, you know ALL FOUR. Always memorise the masculine. That is a 75% discount. Want to test it? Take ста́рый (old). Cut the last two letters: ста́р. Now build: ста́р + ая = ста́рая; ста́р + ое = ста́рое; ста́р + ые = ста́рые. You have just learned four forms of an adjective in three seconds. That is the goal: you build the form, instead of just memorising a ready-made table.

The three masculine endings. Before you use the scissors, you need to know which masculine ending the adjective has. There are three possibilities, and each one tells you which "family" the adjective belongs to. • 1. -ЫЙ (the most common). The vast majority of adjectives. Always -ЫЙ in the masculine: но́вый (new), ста́рый (old), краси́вый (pretty), у́мный (clever), холо́дный (cold), дешёвый (cheap), ве́рный (faithful), дли́нный (long). • 2. -ОЙ (when the stress falls on the ending). You recognise it because the stress is at the end: большо́й (big), молодо́й (young), дорого́й (expensive; dear), плохо́й (bad), просто́й (simple), родно́й (native; dear). Careful: even with -ОЙ, you still cut the last two letters. The stems are БОЛЬШ-, МОЛОД-, ДОРОГ-, ПЛОХ-, ПРОСТ-, РОДН-. • 3. -ИЙ (adjectives with a "special" stem). There are two reasons why an adjective ends in -ИЙ. a) The stem ends in г, к, х (the "throat" consonants). After these consonants Russian never writes Ы; it writes И. That is a spelling rule: ру́сский (Russian), stem РУССК-; ма́ленький (small), stem МАЛЕНЬК-; ди́кий (wild), stem ДИК-; стро́гий (strict), stem СТРОГ-; ти́хий (quiet), stem ТИХ-. In the feminine and neuter these behave like ordinary adjectives: ру́сский → ру́сская → ру́сское; ма́ленький → ма́ленькая → ма́ленькое. b) True "soft" adjectives, the family of синий. A small but important group: си́ний (blue), после́дний (last), у́тренний (morning), вече́рний (evening), весе́нний (spring), зи́мний (winter), ле́тний (summer), осе́нний (autumn). These behave differently: си́ний → си́няя → си́нее (not «си́ная» or «си́ное»!); после́дний → после́дняя → после́днее. This is the only real exception at the start of your studies.

topicos.titulo: The adjective changes with the noun
topicos.explicacao: The adjective comes before the noun and copies its gender and number. To find the form, start from the masculine (-ый, -ий or -ой) and change the ending: feminine -ая (or -яя), neuter -ое (or -ее), plural -ые (or -ие). After г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ you get -ий / -ие (маленький, маленькие, хороший, хорошие). The plural is the same for all three genders. Adjectives come in four types, which only change how the same idea is spelled: hard (-ый), hard with stress on the ending (-ой), after г/к/х/ж/ч/ш/щ (-ий, and neuter -ое when stressed or -ее when unstressed) and soft (-ий, -яя, -ее).
topicos.comparacao: English adjectives never change («a new house», «new books»). In Russian the adjective has a separate form for each of the three genders and another for the plural.

erros.motivo: «Книга» is feminine: so is the adjective.

topicos.titulo: The master table of adjectives and 20 complete adjectives
topicos.explicacao: The master table of adjectives. Here is the table that solves everything. Notice how beautiful the system is: a feminine noun ends in -А/-Я, and the feminine adjective ends in -АЯ/-ЯЯ. A neuter noun ends in -О/-Е, and the neuter adjective ends in -ОЕ/-ЕЕ. A plural noun ends in -Ы/-И, and the plural adjective ends in -ЫЕ/-ИЕ. The system talks to itself: the adjective is a mirror of the noun. If you know the gender of the noun, the adjective slots into place automatically. That is why lesson 11 (noun gender) came before this one. The living table: 20 complete adjectives. Look at the stem of each one. Look at the ending. Notice that the stem never changes. Important notes: • 1. The stem is always the same: НОВ-, СТАР-, БОЛЬШ-, МАЛЕНЬК-, ХОРОШ-, ПЛОХ-, КРАСИВ-, РУССК-, СИН-, ХОЛОДН-, ГОРЯЧ-, ДОРОГ-, ДЕШЁВ-, МОЛОД-, УМН-, ВКУСН-, СЛАДК-, БЕЛ-, ЧЁРН-. • 2. The ending changes with the gender, and you only need to memorise the masculine. • 3. The stress can move. Большо́й → больша́я (the stress moves). Дорого́й → дорога́я (the stress moves). У́мный → у́мная (the stress stays in the same place). This does not affect the ending, but it affects pronunciation. • 4. After the sibilants ж, ч, ш, щ the neuter unstressed ending is spelled -ее, not -ое: хоро́шее, горя́чее. (Same sound as in the soft family, but different reason.)

linhas.MASCULINE: -ИЙ (stem in г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ)

topicos.titulo: The "family of синий": the only real exception
topicos.explicacao: The "family of синий": the only real exception. Among so many -ЫЙ and -ОЙ adjectives lives a small family that ends in -ИЙ and behaves differently. It is the family of синий, the only real exception you need to know at the start. The most common members are in the table. Notice the difference. The feminine is -ЯЯ (not -АЯ): си́няя, not «си́ная». The neuter is -ЕЕ (not -ОЕ): си́нее, not «си́ное». The plural is -ИЕ (not -ЫЕ): си́ние, not «си́ные». How do you recognise them? If the masculine ends in -ИЙ and the stem ends in -н (or another soft consonant), it probably belongs to the family of синий. If the stem ends in г, к, х, it is just spelling forcing -ИЙ (and the feminine is a normal -АЯ). A handy fact: nearly all the members of this family have a time meaning (parts of the day, seasons, "last"). That is a useful pattern for spotting them. And what about третий? It is the other exception. Тре́тий (third) has the feminine тре́тья (not «тре́тия») and the neuter тре́тье (not «тре́тие»). It is a linguistic fossil, a leftover of an old declension. You only have to memorise it.

tabelas.titulo: The "family of синий": the only real exception

topicos.titulo: The big confusion: spelling -ИЙ versus the -ИЙ of the синий family
topicos.explicacao: The big confusion: spelling -ИЙ versus the -ИЙ of the синий family. This point often gets confusing, so let's go slowly. Russian has a spelling rule: after the letters г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ it never writes Ы. It writes И. That is why adjectives like ру́сский (stem РУССК-), ма́ленький (stem МАЛЕНЬК-), ди́кий (stem ДИК-), хоро́ший (stem ХОРОШ-), горя́чий (stem ГОРЯЧ-) end in -ИЙ in the masculine. But they are not from the синий family. How do they behave in the feminine and neuter? Like ordinary adjectives: ру́сский → ру́сская → ру́сское ✅; ма́ленький → ма́ленькая → ма́ленькое ✅; ди́кий → ди́кая → ди́кое ✅; хоро́ший → хоро́шая → хоро́шее ✅; горя́чий → горя́чая → горя́чее ✅. In other words, the feminine is -ая, never -яя. The endings -ИЙ and -ИЕ are only spelling. (One small detail: after ж, ч, ш, щ an unstressed neuter -ое is spelled -ее, which is why you get хоро́шее and горя́чее. That is a spelling matter, not a different declension.) The rule that separates the two groups: if the stem ends in г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ, the -ИЙ is just spelling, so the feminine is -АЯ, the neuter -ОЕ (or -ЕЕ after ж, ч, ш, щ) and the plural -ИЕ. If the stem ends in -н or another soft consonant (the синий family), the -ИЙ is "real", so the feminine is -ЯЯ, the neuter -ЕЕ and the plural -ИЕ. How do you tell them apart in practice? Look at the feminine. If you see "-ая", it is ordinary. If you see "-яя", it is from the синий family. With time you will recognise them. A memory trick: the синий family is small. There are about 15 to 20 adjectives, almost all with a time meaning (seasons, parts of the day) or "last". Everything else that ends in -ИЙ follows the normal -АЯ pattern.

The possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner: «моя книга» is said by a man and by a woman alike. The forms «его» (his), «её» (her) and «их» (their) never change. To say who owns something, put the owner's name in the genitive (the form you use after «нет»): «сумка Лены» = Lena's bag.

её дом, её книга, её окно, её друзья

topicos.titulo: The wandering stress (a trap nobody warns you about)
topicos.explicacao: The wandering stress (a trap nobody warns you about). Here is a trap that is almost never explained clearly: sometimes the stress moves when the ending changes. English does something similar in pairs like "PHOtograph / phoTOgraphy", but in Russian it happens with ordinary grammar. Look: the masculine has the stress on the ending -О́Й. The feminine has the stress on the ending -А́Я. The neuter goes back to -О́Е. The stress wanders. In other adjectives the stress stays still: the stress stays on the stem. There is no fixed rule. You need to listen and memorise. What should you do? Don't try to guess. Copy the form from the table. In time your ear takes over.

tabelas.titulo: The wandering stress (a trap nobody warns you about)

topicos.titulo: First sentences with «это» and adjective traps
topicos.explicacao: First complete sentences: ЭТО. One word, a whole world: э́то (EH-ta), "this is / these are". It never changes, agrees with nothing, and takes care of the present tense of "to be", which in Russian simply does not appear. Your first dialogue in Russian: — Что э́то? (shto EH-ta? What is this?) — Э́то кни́га. (EH-ta KNEE-ga. It is a book.) — Кака́я кни́га? (ka-KAH-ya KNEE-ga? What kind of book?) — Но́вая. (NOH-va-ya. A new one.) And full sentences with everything you have learned. The question "what kind of?" agrees too: како́й? (ka-KOY, masculine), ка́кая? (KAH-ka-ya, feminine), како́е? (ka-KOH-yeh, neuter), каки́е? (ka-KEE-yeh, plural). — Како́й дом? — Но́вый. (What kind of house? A new one.) — Кака́я кни́га? — Но́вая. (What kind of book? A new one.) — Како́е пи́во? — Холо́дное. (What kind of beer? Cold.) Classic traps (spotted in advance, so you don't fall into them). ⚠ Mistake 1: choosing the gender by meaning. In English "the new house" and "the new book" use the same adjective, so you might not think about it at all. In Russian the adjective must match: ❌ нова́я дом. To a Russian, «нова́я дом» sounds as wrong as "a new houses" sounds to you. ✅ но́вый дом, because дом is masculine. And "a new book"? ✅ но́вая кни́га, because кни́га is feminine. ⚠ Mistake 2: touching the stem. ❌ «новова́я». The scissors cut exactly two letters. The stem is untouchable. ⚠ Mistake 3: forgetting that -мя is neuter. ❌ но́вый вре́мя → ✅ но́вое вре́мя (вре́мя is neuter). ⚠ Mistake 4: mixing up the синий family. ❌ си́ная мо́ре → ✅ си́нее мо́ре (мо́ре is neuter, and the neuter of синий is -ЕЕ). ❌ си́ная кни́га → ✅ си́няя кни́га (синий has the feminine -ЯЯ, not -АЯ). ⚠ Mistake 5: using -ЯЯ on adjectives with a stem in к, ш, г, х. ❌ ру́сскяя → ✅ ру́сская (the stem РУССК- ends in к; -ИЙ is only spelling, the feminine is -АЯ). ❌ хоро́шяя → ✅ хоро́шая (the stem ХОРОШ- ends in ш; -ИЙ is only spelling, the feminine is -АЯ). ⚠ Mistake 6: looking for articles. "A new house" and "the new house" are, in Russian, the same thing: но́вый дом. The articles are gone and the context does their job. Breathe out: the eternal "a or the?" question is over. The difficulty has moved to agreement, and agreement you now know how to do.

A curiosity: кра́сный (red) and краси́вый (beautiful) are relatives. In Old Russian "red" also meant "beautiful", which is why Red Square is, at heart, "Beautiful Square". STEP 1: • 1. An adjective completes a noun. It is stem + ending. STEP 2: • 2. The stem never changes. The ending changes to agree. STEP 3: • 3. You only memorise the masculine. The other three forms come for free. STEP 4: • 4. The "scissors" method: cut off the last two letters of the masculine, paste on the new ending. STEP 5: • 5. Three masculine endings: STEP 6: -ЫЙ (common) STEP 7: -ОЙ (stress on the ending) STEP 8: -ИЙ (after г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ, or the синий family) STEP 9: • 6. Feminine endings: -АЯ (common) or -ЯЯ (синий family). STEP 10: • 7. Neuter endings: -ОЕ (common) or -ЕЕ (синий family). STEP 11: • 8. The синий family is the only real exception: си́ний → си́няя → си́нее → си́ние. STEP 12: • 9. Adjectives in -ИЙ after г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ do not belong to the синий family: ру́сский → ру́сская, хоро́ший → хоро́шая. STEP 13: • 10. The stress can move: большо́й → больша́я → большо́е. Do not try to guess. Copy it from the table. STEP 14: • 11. Э́то never changes and replaces the verb to be in the present tense.

topicos.titulo: The adverb: the word that never changes
topicos.explicacao: An adverb is a word that tells you HOW, WHEN, WHERE or HOW MUCH something happens: «well», «today», «here», «very». It never changes its form, not for gender and not for plural. That is the difference from the adjective: «хороший дом» (adjective: it changes with the noun) × «Он хорошо работает» (adverb: always «хорошо»). Many adverbs are born from an adjective: drop the ending (-ый, -ий, -ой) and add -о. Others are words in their own right: здесь, там, сейчас, очень, всегда.
topicos.comparacao: «quick» → «quickly», «slow» → «slowly». The idea is the same as in English: the adverb comes from the adjective and does not vary. In English you add -ly; in Russian you just swap the ending for -о.

erros.motivo: After a verb, use the adverb, which does not change.
To say HOW someone does something, use an adverb.

topicos.explicacao: The adverbs of frequency form a scale: всегда (always), часто (often), иногда (sometimes), редко (rarely), никогда (never). In Russian, when «никогда» is there, the verb takes «не» as well: «Я никогда не читаю», literally «I never don't read». In English we say just «I never read». This is called the double negative, and in Russian it is compulsory.
topicos.comparacao: Non-standard English also stacks negatives («I don't never read»), but in Russian this is the standard rule: «не» is always required.

topicos.explicacao: Yes/no question: keep the sentence as it is and raise your voice at the end: «Ты студент?» There is no word-order inversion and no «do/does», and «есть» is not used. Answer: «Да.» or «Нет.» Question with a question word: put the word at the beginning: «Где ты живёшь?», «Когда ты работаешь?». The word «какой» agrees with the noun, like an adjective. To answer «почему», begin with «потому что».
topicos.comparacao: English can ask a question with intonation alone, too («You're a student?»), but only informally. In Russian this is the normal way to ask every yes/no question.

erros.motivo: Yes/no question: same sentence, rising intonation. No «есть».

tabela.question: какой
tabela.exemplo: Какой это дом? Какая это книга?

topicos.explicacao: A scene you have lived (or will). Picture it. You are in Russia. You have studied the alphabet, nouns, adjectives, verbs in the present, past and future. You feel confident. You walk into a shop, point at something and say: — Я ви́жу кни́га. The shop assistant understands, but winces. She repeats it, correcting you: — Я ви́жу кни́гу. You look again. It is the same word, кни́га, but now it ends in -у, not -а. You think: "Why? I learned that кни́га is feminine. Why did the ending change?" This happens to every Russian learner, and it happens because you have just met the accusative case. It sounds complicated, but it is not. Five minutes of careful reading will save you years of false immersion. What English already does. English has almost no cases, but it keeps a trace of this one in its pronouns. You say "I see him", never "I see he". You say "She loves me", never "She loves I". "Him", "her", "me", "us", "them", "whom" are the accusative (the object form) of he, she, I, we, they, who. Russian does the same with pronouns (я → меня, он → его), and, unlike English, it does it with nouns too. The case of action. The accusative is the case of the thing the action is done to. When you say "I read the book", "the book" is the object of the action. In English you know it is the object only because of word order (it comes after the verb). Russian lets the ending carry that job, which is why the word order can be freer. This object needs a special mark in Russian. That mark is the accusative case.

topicos.titulo: Animate and inanimate: who "has a soul"
topicos.explicacao: The Russian view: who has a soul? Now comes the most fascinating part. Pay attention, because here is the key to everything. In Russian grammar, only people and animals "have a soul" (this is the traditional teaching image; grammarians call it animate versus inanimate). People have a soul. Animals have a soul. Objects don't. Plants don't. Ideas don't. A house has no soul. A stone has no soul. But a friend does. A dog does. A child does. What does this have to do with grammar? Everything. Because only those with a soul get special treatment in the accusative. Only they change form when they are the object of the action. I'll explain with the magic question: does the word have a soul? If YES → it is "animate" and gets a special mark in the accusative (in the masculine). If NO → it is "inanimate" and does not change in the accusative (in the masculine). Examples: Does Дом (house) have a soul? No. A house is an object, so it does not change in the accusative. Стол (table)? No, so it does not change. Друг (friend)? Yes, a person, so it changes in the accusative. Студент (student)? Yes, a person, so it changes. Собака (dog)? Yes, an animal. But wait: «собака» is feminine, and for the feminine the rule is different. We will get there. Keep this question in your head. It will solve 90% of your accusative mistakes. The single rule that solves it all. Before the details, here is the rule in one sentence. Memorise it: FEMININE: ALWAYS CHANGES. It makes no difference whether it has a soul or not. Always. MASCULINE: DEPENDS ON THE SOUL. If it has a soul, it changes. If not, it does not change. NEUTER: NEVER CHANGES. It is neuter, by nature. That is all. Three lines. You have just learned the accusative of nouns. Now the details.

The FEMININE: it always changes. The feminine is the easiest because it is consistent. It always changes, whether it has a soul or not. Feminine ending in -А → becomes -У. You drop the -а and put -у. As simple as that. Feminine ending in -Я → becomes -Ю. You drop the -я and put -ю. As simple as that. Feminine ending in -Ь → DOES NOT CHANGE. The feminine in -ь stays the same as the nominative. Attention: how do you know whether a feminine word will change? Look at the ending. Ends in -а → changes to -у. Ends in -я → changes to -ю. Ends in -ь → no change. And the soul? For the feminine it does not matter. The rule is always the same, with a soul or without. That is why the feminine is the easiest.

tabelas.titulo: The FEMININE in -а: it changes to -у
The FEMININE in -я: it changes to -ю

topicos.titulo: Case: the function of a word in the sentence
topicos.explicacao: In English, the function of a word shows in word order and prepositions: «the dog bit the man» is not «the man bit the dog». In Russian, the function shows in the ending: the word changes its ending, and each ending is a case. There are six cases. In «Мама читает книгу», «мама» is who does the action (nominative) and «книгу» is what receives the action (accusative). You have already used four of the six cases without knowing their names; now they get names.
topicos.comparacao: English does not change its nouns, but it does change its pronouns: «I / me», «he / him». Russian does this with every word.

erros.motivo: The direct object goes into the accusative.

tabela.question: Кто? Что?
tabela.funcao: who does it; the dictionary form

tabela.question: Кому? Чему?
tabela.funcao: to whom, for whom (coming up next)

tabela.question: Кем? Чем?
tabela.funcao: with whom, by means of (coming up next)

topicos.titulo: The MASCULINE: it depends on the soul
topicos.explicacao: The MASCULINE: it depends on the soul. Now the masculine. Here the magic question comes in: does it have a soul? Masculine INANIMATE (no soul) → DOES NOT CHANGE. If the word is masculine and has no soul (an object, an idea, a place, a thing), it does not change in the accusative. It stays the same as the nominative. Notice: the word is identical. Дом is дом in the nominative and in the accusative. Example sentences follow. All inanimate objects stay the same: no mark, no change. Masculine ANIMATE (with a soul) → CHANGES (add one letter). If the word is masculine and has a soul (a person or an animal), it changes in the accusative. The change: add -А at the end (or -Я, if the word ends in -ь or -й). Rule: a masculine animate word ending in a consonant → +А. A masculine animate word ending in -ь → becomes -Я. A masculine animate word ending in -й → becomes -Я. Notice that you don't cut any letter. You add one at the end, -А or -Я. Example sentences follow. Notice that every word with a soul changed, and every one added a letter. The magic question in practice. Here is how to use the magic question to decide whether a masculine word changes. That is all. Ask. Answer. Apply. (Note that the animate masculine accusative is the same as the genitive: you will meet that in the next lessons.)

linhas.TRANSLATION: We are waiting for the doctor.

topicos.titulo: The neuter, the master table and the accusative rule
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The NEUTER: it never changes. The neuter is the easiest of all. It never changes in the accusative. It makes no difference whether it is an object, an idea or a thing. It stays the same as the nominative. Always. Notice that no neuter word changes. Ever. Example sentences follow. That is it. The neuter is neuter: no soul, no masculine/feminine endings to swap, no change. Full stop. STEP 2: The master table of the accusative. Here is the table that solves everything. STEP 3: The rule in three lines. If you forget everything else, memorise this: FEMININE: ALWAYS CHANGES (а→у, я→ю, ь does not change). MASCULINE: ASK "HAS IT GOT A SOUL?". If yes, add -а/-я. If not, no change. NEUTER: NEVER CHANGES. That is it. You have just mastered the accusative of nouns.

tabelas.titulo: The master table of the accusative

linhas.EXAMPLE: дом → дом; музе́й → музе́й; слова́рь → слова́рь
окно́ → окно́; мо́ре → мо́ре; вре́мя → вре́мя

topicos.titulo: Genitive: how to form it and when to use it
topicos.explicacao: The genitive answers «кого? чего?». You use it (1) to say something does not exist: «У меня нет сестры»; (2) to say the owner: «книга брата»; (3) to say the origin: «из Бразилии»; (4) after certain prepositions: у, из, от, для, без, около, после; (5) with quantities: «чашка кофе». Formation in the singular: -а becomes -ы; -я becomes -и; a final consonant gains -а; masculine -й and -ь become -я; -о becomes -а; -е becomes -я; feminine -ь becomes -и. After г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ you write -и, never -ы.

topicos.titulo: Special cases (мать, дочь) and support tables for the accusative
topicos.explicacao: Special cases. МАТЬ and ДОЧЬ. Two feminine words in -ь. In the singular they behave like any other feminine in -ь: they do not change. Мать is мать, дочь is дочь. In the plural they are irregular: the accusative plural is матере́й and дочере́й (the same as the genitive plural). You only need to remember this when you reach the plural. ДИТЯ. Дитя́ (child) is the only neuter word that names a person. In the accusative singular it stays дитя́ (the same as the nominative). In the plural it is дете́й (the same as the genitive plural). It is an exception, but you already know that дитя is special. СУДЬЯ. Судья́ (judge) is masculine in meaning but feminine in form (it ends in -я). In the accusative it changes like a feminine noun: судью́. Support tables: personal pronouns, adjectives and possessives in the accusative. English comparison: this is the part English still has. Just as "he" becomes "him" and "she" becomes "her", Russian я becomes меня́ and она́ becomes её.

tabelas.titulo: Support table: personal pronouns in the accusative

linhas.PRACTICAL EXAMPLE: Ты понима́ешь меня́? (Do you understand me?) · Я люблю́ тебя́. (I love you.)
Я зна́ю его́. (I know him.) · Он ви́дит её. (He sees her.)
Они́ ждут нас. (They are waiting for us.) · Мы зна́ем их. (We know them.)

tabelas.titulo: Support table: adjectives and possessives in the accusative

topicos.titulo: Common accusative mistakes, sentences and summary chart
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistakes English speakers WILL make in the accusative. Mistake 1: using the nominative instead of the accusative for a feminine noun. ❌ Wrong: Я ви́жу кни́га. ✅ Right: Я ви́жу кни́гу. English nouns never change after the verb, so you think "book is book". But a feminine noun always changes in Russian. Always. Mistake 2: not changing an animate masculine. ❌ Wrong: Я ви́жу друг. ✅ Right: Я ви́жу дру́га. A "friend" has a soul. It changes. Always. Mistake 3: changing an inanimate masculine. ❌ Wrong: Я ви́жу до́ма. ✅ Right: Я ви́жу дом. A "house" has no soul. It does not change. Never. Mistake 4: forgetting that the neuter never changes. ❌ Wrong: Я ви́жу окна́. ✅ Right: Я ви́жу окно́. The neuter never changes. Never. Mistake 5: thinking that the feminine in -ь changes. ❌ Wrong: Я ви́жу дверю́. ✅ Right: Я ви́жу дверь. The feminine in -ь stays the same as the nominative. Mistake 6: applying the animate-masculine rule to a feminine word that names an animal. ❌ Wrong: Я ви́жу соба́к. The dog has a soul, so you might want to add a letter like for a masculine. But соба́ка is feminine, and a feminine always follows the feminine rule: а → у. ✅ Right: Я ви́жу соба́ку. The soul only matters for masculine nouns. Mistake 7: not telling an animate masculine from an inanimate one. This is the most serious error. Both стол and друг end in a consonant, and you cannot see the difference by looking. The magic question solves it: does стол have a soul? No. Does друг have a soul? Yes. STEP 2: Full sentences with the accusative. Now real sentences, to see the accusative at work. STEP 3: Summary chart: the accusative case.

linhas.TRANSLATION: We are waiting for the doctor.

topicos.titulo: Dative and instrumental: just the essentials
topicos.explicacao: The dative answers «кому?» (to whom, for whom): masculine -у or -ю (брат → брату), feminine -е (мама → маме). The pronouns change a lot: я → мне, ты → тебе, он → ему, она → ей, мы → нам, вы → вам, они → им. One important sentence: «Мне нравится музыка» (literally «to me is pleasing the music» = I like music). The instrumental answers «кем?» and is the form for «with someone» (with = «с»): masculine -ом or -ем (брат → с братом), feminine -ой or -ей (мама → с мамой). This is only a first contact: each case will get its own lessons.

exemplos.pt: I give the book to my brother.

topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: • 1. The accusative is the case of ACTION. It is the case of the object: what is seen, read, said, eaten, loved, written. STEP 2: • 2. For Russian grammar, only human beings and animals count as "animate". This decides which words change in the accusative and which do not. STEP 3: • 3. The rule in three lines: STEP 4: FEMININE: ALWAYS CHANGES. (а→у, я→ю, ь does not change) STEP 5: MASCULINE: ASK "IS IT ANIMATE?". If yes, add -а/-я. If not, no change. STEP 6: NEUTER: NEVER CHANGES. STEP 7: • 4. The magic question: is a house animate? No → no change. Is a friend animate? Yes → it changes. STEP 8: • 5. Feminine in -а → -у (кни́га → кни́гу). STEP 9: • 6. Feminine in -я → -ю (семья́ → семью́). STEP 10: • 7. Feminine in -ь → no change (ночь → ночь). STEP 11: • 8. Masculine inanimate → no change (дом → дом). STEP 12: • 9. Masculine animate ending in a consonant → +а (друг → дру́га). STEP 13: • 10. Masculine animate ending in -ь or -й → -я (медве́дь → медве́дя; геро́й → геро́я). STEP 14: • 11. Neuter → never changes (окно́ → окно́; мо́ре → мо́ре; вре́мя → вре́мя). STEP 15: Plural: inanimate = same as the nominative (столы́ → столы́, города́ → города́); animate = same as the genitive plural.
