topicos.titulo: What is a verb? The "happening" test
topicos.explicacao: What is a verb? The "happening" test. Before any table, the basic question: what is a verb? A verb is the word that expresses an action, a state or an occurrence. It is what a person does, is or experiences. And there is a reliable test to recognise it, the "happening" test: "I ___ at home." → live, am, stay → verb. "He ___ Russian." → speaks, studies, learns → verb. "We ___ books." → read, buy, write → verb. The verb is the backbone of the sentence. Without a verb there is no action. Without a verb there is no complete sentence. You already know how to say "Э́то но́вый дом" (this is a new house). But you cannot yet say "I am building a new house" or "He lives in a new house". That is the subject of this lesson. And the good news? The Russian verb is much more regular than you think. Much more than the noun or the adjective. The exceptions are few, and the rules are consistent. You will see.

What is a subject pronoun? (the simple truth, no fear). Before you conjugate any verb, you need to know what it is conjugated with. That means knowing the subject pronouns. "Subject pronoun" may sound like a grammar monster, but it is the simplest thing in the world. Let me take the name apart: Pronoun = a word that replaces a noun. Instead of "John" you say "he". Instead of "Mary" you say "she". Subject = it is the doer of the action in the sentence. In English, the subject pronouns are: In Russian, they are: That is all. You have used "I, you, he, she" all your life. Russian is the same: you only have to learn the matching words. No terror, no absurd memorising. Five minutes of attention is enough. Important details: • 1. Ты vs. вы. In Russian, ты is used with friends, family, children and close people. Вы is used with strangers, older people, authorities, and always for the plural. English has only "you" for both, so you must choose. • 2. Он, она́, оно́. In Russian, everything has a gender, even objects. So "table" (стол) is masculine → он; "house" (дом) is masculine → он; "book" (кни́га) is feminine → она́; "window" (окно́) is neuter → оно́. English says "it" for all of these. This is scary at first, but you already learned in lesson 11 that gender is determined by the last letter. Now you just apply it: if the noun is masculine, use он; if feminine, она́; if neuter, оно́. • 3. Они́. A single form for all three genders in the plural. It does not matter whether it is "they" (men) or "they" (women). It is always они́.

topicos.titulo: What is conjugation? (the clearest explanation you will read)
topicos.explicacao: What is conjugation? (the clearest explanation you will read). Before anything else, a question nobody asks and everybody should: what does it mean to conjugate a verb? To conjugate is to change the form of the verb to match the subject of the sentence. English does this very little (I speak, he speaks); Russian does it for every person. Look: Notice that the stem speak- is always the same. Only the ending changes (here just -s in the third person). You never thought "I invented a new stem" when you wrote "speaks". You just changed the ending. That is conjugating. Russian works on exactly the same principle. You have a stem (which carries the meaning) and an ending (which carries the person). The stem never changes. The ending changes. ЧИТА- + -Ю = чита́ю (I read) ЧИТА- + -ЕШЬ = чита́ешь (you read) ЧИТА- + -ЕТ = чита́ет (he / she reads) ЧИТА- + -ЕМ = чита́ем (we read) ЧИТА- + -ЕТЕ = чита́ете (you read, plural or formal) ЧИТА- + -ЮТ = чита́ют (they read) The stem ЧИТА- never changed. Only the ending. Always. The difference from English is that Russian has a different ending for every person, and that is what scares beginners. But the mechanics are simple. You have just learned to conjugate a Russian verb. That is it. The rest is practice.

The verb "scissors": the method nobody teaches. Just as we did with the adjective (lesson 12), we will apply the scissors to the verb. Remember this: every Russian verb is a LEGO of two pieces: STEM (untouchable) + ENDING (movable). And the method is always the same: • 1. Find the infinitive (the "dictionary" form, which ends in -ТЬ, -ТИ or -ЧЬ). • 2. Cut off the infinitive ending (-ТЬ, -ТИ, -ЧЬ). You have the stem. • 3. Paste on the personal ending (-Ю, -ЕШЬ, -ЕТ, -ЕМ, -ЕТЕ, -ЮТ or -Ю, -ИШЬ, -ИТ, -ИМ, -ИТЕ, -ЯТ). Done. The verb is conjugated. See it in practice with чита́ть (to read): • 1. Infinitive: чита́ть • 2. Cut -ТЬ: чита́ (stem) • 3. Paste the endings: чита́ + ю = чита́ю (I read) чита́ + ешь = чита́ешь (you read) чита́ + ет = чита́ет (he reads) чита́ + ем = чита́ем (we read) чита́ + ете = чита́ете (you read, plural or formal) чита́ + ют = чита́ют (they read) And with говори́ть (to speak): • 1. Infinitive: говори́ть • 2. Cut -ТЬ: говори́- • 3. Paste the endings: говор + ю = говорю́ (I speak) говори́ + шь = говори́шь (you speak) говори́ + т = говори́т (he speaks) говори́ + м = говори́м (we speak) говори́ + те = говори́те (you speak, plural or formal) говор + ят = говоря́т (they speak). Notice: in the verb говори́ть, the vowel -и- stays in most forms (говор-и-шь) but disappears before -ю and -ят (говор-ю, говор-ят). That is normal. Why does this help? Because the Russian verb works like LEGO: instead of memorising the table, you learn to build each form. The Russian infinitive: three endings. In Russian, the infinitive (the "dictionary" form) ends in three different ways: The good news: you do not need to worry about -ТИ and -ЧЬ now. They are a minority. The vast majority of verbs end in -ТЬ, and that is what we study in this lesson.

tabelas.titulo: The Russian infinitive: the three endings

linhas.EXAMPLES: чита́ть, говори́ть, писа́ть, жить, знать, понима́ть, рабо́тать, люби́ть, смотре́ть, слу́шать

topicos.titulo: The two conjugations: the logic behind them
topicos.explicacao: The two conjugations: the logic behind them. Here is a point that tends to stay unclear. Let us clear it up. In Russian, verbs fall into two conjugations. And the difference between them is in the personal endings: 1st CONJUGATION: 2nd CONJUGATION: How do you decide which conjugation to use? Look at the ending of the infinitive: Verbs in -ать and -ять → almost always 1st conjugation. Verbs in -ить → almost always 2nd conjugation. Verbs in -еть → mostly 2nd (смотреть, видеть, сидеть), with exceptions such as болеть and уметь. Examples: чита́ть (to read) → ends in -ать → 1st conjugation → чита́ю, чита́ешь, чита́ет... гуля́ть (to take a walk) → -ять → 1st conjugation → гуля́ю, гуля́ешь, гуля́ет... боле́ть (to hurt, to be ill) → -еть → 1st conjugation (an exception) → боле́ю, боле́ешь, боле́ет... говори́ть (to speak) → -ить → 2nd conjugation → говорю́, говори́шь, говори́т... люби́ть (to love) → -ить → 2nd conjugation → люблю́, лю́бишь, лю́бит... звони́ть (to phone) → -ить → 2nd conjugation → звоню́, звони́шь, звони́т... Careful: there are exceptions. Some verbs in -ать, -ять, -еть belong to the 2nd conjugation. There are only eleven, and I will list them later.

To conjugate is to change the end of the verb to show WHO does the action: I speak, you speak, he speaks. English only changes the verb in the third person singular (speak → speaks). Russian changes it for every person. The Russian present tense has only TWO conjugations, and each has its own endings. Step by step: (1) drop the -ть from the infinitive to find the stem; (2) find out the conjugation of the verb; (3) add the six endings. 1st conjugation: -ю, -ешь, -ет, -ем, -ете, -ют (after a consonant, -у and -ут). 2nd conjugation: -ю, -ишь, -ит, -им, -ите, -ят (after ж, ч, ш, щ, -у and -ат). The difference is in the vowel: е in the 1st, и in the 2nd.
topicos.comparacao: an English infinitive («to speak») tells you nothing about the endings. The Russian infinitive in -ть alone is not enough either: you must learn the conjugation together with the verb; the next session gives the practical rules.

topicos.titulo: The four types of verb in the present
topicos.explicacao: The four types of verb in the present. To make them easier to memorise, let's sort the present-tense verbs into four types. Type 1: ЗНАТЬ (the most common). Verbs in -ать and -ять (plus a few in -еть, such as уметь) that take the endings -ю, -ешь, -ет, -ем, -ете, -ют. Type 2: ГОВОРИТЬ (verbs in -ить and most verbs in -еть). They take the endings -ю, -ишь, -ит, -им, -ите, -ят. Type 1B: ЖИТЬ (verbs whose stem ends in a consonant). They take endings similar to the first conjugation, but with -у in the first person singular (instead of -ю). Attention: when the stress falls on the ending, the letter е becomes ё (живёшь, живёт, живём, живёте). That does not change the ending, only the pronunciation; it is a spelling convention. Type 2B: irregular verbs (few, but important). хоте́ть (to want): хочу́, хо́чешь, хо́чет, хоти́м, хоти́те, хотя́т. This verb is a mixture of both conjugations. есть (to eat): ем, ешь, ест, еди́м, еди́те, едя́т. пить (to drink): пью, пьёшь, пьёт, пьём, пьёте, пьют. дать (to give): дам, дашь, даст, дади́м, дади́те, даду́т. English has almost no verb endings (only -s in "he works"), so Russian looks heavy at first. The good news: there are only two main sets of endings, and you can choose between them by looking at the infinitive.

tabelas.titulo: Type 2: the verbs in -ить and most in -еть
Type 1B and other verbs with a consonant stem

topicos.titulo: Exceptions: 11 verbs in -ать/-ять/-еть of the 2nd conjugation
topicos.explicacao: The exceptions: the 11 verbs in -ать/-ять/-еть that go to the 2nd conjugation. Here is a list few materials give. There are eleven verbs that end in -ать, -ять or -еть but do not follow the 1st conjugation. They follow the 2nd. How to memorise them? A tip: almost all of these verbs have a connotation of perception (see, hear, look, breathe) or feeling (hate, offend, endure). It is not an absolute rule, but it helps. Memorise them.

tabelas.titulo: The 11 exceptions in -ать/-ять/-еть that go to the 2nd conjugation

topicos.titulo: The stress that wanders (or stays put)
topicos.explicacao: The stress that wanders (or stays put). As with the adjective, the stress of the verb can move, or stay in the same place. Look: • 1. Stress fixed on the stem (most common in the 1st conjugation): • 2. Stress fixed on the ending (common in the 2nd conjugation): • 3. Stress that wanders (a minority): What should you do? Do not try to guess. Copy the form from the table. With time, your ear takes over. And remember: if the verb contains ё, the stress always falls on the ё. That is why живёшь, живёт, живём, живёте.

tabelas.titulo: Stress on the ending, or moving to the stem after «я»

topicos.titulo: The verb TO BE (быть): the most famous absence in Russian
topicos.explicacao: The verb TO BE (быть): the most famous absence in Russian. This is the biggest surprise for English speakers. Pay attention. In Russian, the verb TO BE (быть) does not exist in the present tense. In English we say: I am Brazilian. He is a doctor. We are students. In Russian, the verb disappears: Я брази́лец. (I Brazilian.) Он врач. (He doctor.) Мы студе́нты. (We students.) The verb "to be" simply does not appear. The context does its job. It is as if the sentence were "I Brazilian", "He doctor". Russian does not miss it at all. But note one exception: the 3rd person singular of быть — есть — survives with a special meaning: "there is", "exists", "has". This is the form you will use in the construction for "to have" (next section).

topicos.titulo: How to say "I have", "you have", "he has"
topicos.explicacao: How to say "I have", "you have", "he has". This is one of the biggest differences between English and Russian, and one of the first things you will want to say. Pay attention. In everyday Russian there is no verb "to have" like the English one. Instead, Russian uses a construction that, translated literally, means "by me there is": У меня́ есть кни́га. = I have a book. (Literally: "By me there is a book".) Let me take the formula apart: У = a preposition meaning "by", "at the place of", "in the possession of". меня́ = "me" (a special form of the pronoun "I" used after у). есть = "there is", "exists" (the surviving form of the verb to be). кни́га = "book" (the thing possessed). The structure is always the same. See it with all the pronouns: Notice how the pronoun changes after у: Why does it change? It is a grammar matter you will understand later, when we study the cases. For now, memorise the forms as a formula. That is how it is said. Full stop. The good news: the formula is fixed. Always у + special form + есть + object. No mystery. Can the word "есть" be left out? Yes, in informal contexts or when the possession is obvious: У меня́ кни́га. (I have a book.) У тебя́ вре́мя? (Do you have time?) But in general, use есть while you are learning. Russians understand perfectly and you will not risk sounding odd. How to negate: To say "I don't have", Russian uses нет instead of есть: У меня́ нет кни́ги. (I don't have a book.) У тебя́ нет вре́мени? (Don't you have time?) У него́ нет маши́ны. (He doesn't have a car.) Careful: the word after нет changes form. That is a subject for a future lesson. For now, memorise the most common examples: The logic is: when affirmative, use есть + the normal object; when negative, use нет + a "modified" object. You will learn how to modify it later, but you can already memorise these ready-made formulas.

tabelas.titulo: I have, you have, he has

topicos.explicacao: Complete sentences: the first dialogues. Now that you know the subject pronouns, the two conjugations, the absence of the verb to be and the construction for "to have", you can form complete sentences. Dialogue 1 — In class: — Что ты де́лаешь? (What are you doing?) — Я чита́ю кни́гу. (I am reading a book.) — А он? (And he?) — Он пи́шет упражне́ние. (He is writing an exercise.) — А они́? (And they?) — Они́ говоря́т по-ру́сски. (They are speaking Russian.) Dialogue 2 — At home: — Где ты живёшь? (Where do you live?) — Я живу́ в Москве́. (I live in Moscow.) — А твоя́ семья́? (And your family?) — Они́ живу́т в Санкт-Петербу́рге. (They live in St Petersburg.) Dialogue 3 — At work: — Кто э́то? (Who is this?) — Э́то мой друг. Он рабо́тает здесь. (This is my friend. He works here.) — Он зна́ет ру́сский язы́к? (Does he know Russian?) — Да, немно́го. (Yes, a little.) Dialogue 4 — The verb "to have": — У тебя́ есть вре́мя? (Do you have time?) — Да, есть. А что? (Yes, I do. Why?) — У меня́ есть вопро́с. (I have a question.) — Хорошо́, спра́шивай. (All right, ask.) Dialogue 5 — Introducing yourself: — Приве́т! Как тебя́ зову́т? (Hi! What is your name?) — Меня́ зову́т Ива́н. А тебя́? (My name is Ivan. And yours?) — Меня́ зову́т Мари́я. Я изуча́ю ру́сский язы́к. (My name is Maria. I study Russian.) — Я то́же изуча́ю ру́сский. (I also study Russian.) Note: "Как тебя́ зову́т?" literally means "How do they call you?": the verb звать (to call) is in the 3rd person plural. The answer is Меня́ зову́т... ("They call me..."). It is the fixed formula for "What is your name?" in Russian. Memorise it as a block.

topicos.titulo: How to recognise the conjugation from the infinitive
topicos.explicacao: Practical rules: verbs in -ить are 2nd conjugation (говорить, любить, платить). Verbs in -еть are almost all 2nd conjugation (смотреть, видеть, сидеть), with exceptions such as «уметь» (умею) and «хотеть» (mixed). Verbs in -ать and -ять are almost all 1st conjugation (читать, делать, гулять), except a few 2nd-conjugation exceptions: слышать, держать, дышать, лежать, стоять. Verbs in -овать and -евать are 1st conjugation and change to -ую (рисовать → рисую). Verbs in -авать are 1st conjugation (вставать → встаю). In the 2nd conjugation, some consonants change ONLY in the «я» form: б → бл (любить → люблю), в → вл (готовить → готовлю), д → ж (видеть → вижу), т → ч (платить → плачу), с → ш (просить → прошу). The other forms stay regular: любишь, видишь.

erros.motivo: In the 2nd conjugation, б becomes бл in the «я» form.
д becomes ж in the «я» form.

tabelas.titulo: Consonant change only in the «я» form (2nd conjugation)

linhas.exemplo: видеть → я вижу, ты видишь; ходить → я хожу, ты ходишь

topicos.titulo: ADVERBS: the words that never change
topicos.explicacao: ADVERBS: the words that never change. Before we close this lesson, I need to introduce a class of words that will give you huge relief: adverbs. I'll be direct: the adverb is the easiest class of words in the whole of Russian. I am not exaggerating, and you will see why in three minutes. What is an adverb? An adverb is a word that modifies the verb. It tells you how, when, where or how often the action happens. You use adverbs all the time in English: I read quickly (how?). We arrived today (when?). He lives here (where?). She always studies (how often?). Quickly, today, here, always: all adverbs. They attach to the verb and tell you how, when or where the action happens. The big news: the adverb is INVARIABLE. Now pay attention to this word: invariable. It means: it does not change. Ever. For any reason. Let me prove it with concrete examples. Proof 1: the adverb does not change with gender. Take the English adverb "today". Does it change if the speaker is a man or a woman? "I am happy today" is the same for both. There is no "todayess" for a woman. Russian is the same. The adverb сего́дня (today) is always сего́дня, whether the speaker is a man, a woman, a child or an adult. Proof 2: the adverb does not change with number. Take "here". Does it change if one person or several are here? "I am here. We are here." No. "Here" is "here" for one or for a thousand. Russian is the same: здесь is always здесь. Proof 3: the adverb does not change with tense. Take "yesterday". It does not become anything else when the verb changes. Russian is the same. The adverb вчера́ (yesterday) is always вчера́. What changes is the verb, not the adverb: in the past tense «читал» changes to «читала» for a woman, but вчера́ stays put. The golden rule of the adverb: an adverb is a frozen word. It does not change with gender, number, person, tense or case. It is always the same form, in any sentence, with any subject, in any context. That is why the adverb is the easiest class in Russian. While nouns, adjectives and verbs change form, adverbs stand still. If you like memorising, memorise adverbs. There are no tricks, no exceptions, no conjugation. It is the only class in Russian where you can learn a word and use it for ever without fear. Some essential adverbs. Here are the most used adverbs in everyday life; notice that all are invariable. Time. Place. Manner. How to use adverbs in sentences. The position of the adverb is flexible. Generally: an adverb of time goes before the verb or at the start of the sentence. An adverb of place goes after the verb. An adverb of manner goes after the verb. Examples follow. Notice that the adverb never changes form, whatever the sentence. Хорошо́ is always хорошо́. Сего́дня is always сего́дня. Здесь is always здесь. You do not need to think about gender, number, person or tense. Just drop the word in. Comparison with English: you already do this. In English the adverb is invariable too: I speak well. She speaks well. We speak well. They speak well. "Well" is always "well". The difference: in English many adverbs are made from adjectives by adding "-ly" (slow → slowly, quick → quickly). In Russian many adverbs are made from adjectives by changing the ending to -о (or -е): хоро́ший → хорошо́, бы́стрый → бы́стро. But that is only the origin of the adverb. Once formed, it stands still. Хорошо́ does not become anything else for a woman or for a plural. It is always хорошо́. Full stop. An important remark: adverb versus neuter adjective. Be careful not to confuse the adverb with the neuter adjective. They can have the same form but different jobs. Он хорошо́ говори́т. (He speaks well.) → хорошо́ is an adverb: it modifies the verb говори́т. Э́то хоро́шее вино́. (This is a good wine.) → хоро́шее is a neuter adjective: it modifies the noun вино́. The difference is in the job: if it modifies a verb, it is an adverb; if it modifies a noun, it is an adjective. Context makes this clear. Quick exercise. Complete with the right adverb. • 1. Я ____ чита́ю. (now) • 2. Он ____ рабо́тает. (today) • 3. Мы бу́дем ____ в Москве́. (tomorrow) • 4. Я был ____ в теа́тре. (yesterday) • 5. Она́ живёт ____. (there) • 6. Он ____ чита́ет. (here) • 7. Я ____. (at home) • 8. Она́ ____ говори́т по-ру́сски. (well) • 9. Он ____ чита́ет. (slowly) • 10. Они́ ____ рабо́тают. (always) Answer key: • 1. сейча́с • 2. сего́дня • 3. за́втра • 4. вчера́ • 5. там • 6. здесь (or тут) • 7. до́ма • 8. хорошо́ • 9. ме́дленно • 10. всегда́. Pocket summary: adverbs. • 1. An adverb is a word that modifies the verb (it says how, when, where, how often). • 2. The adverb is invariable. It does not change with gender, number, person, tense or case. • 3. "Today" is today for a man, a woman, a child, an adult. Always. • 4. "Here" is here for one person or a thousand. Always. • 5. "Well" is well for any subject. Always. • 6. If you like memorising, memorise adverbs. They are the easiest class in Russian: no conjugation, no declension, no tricks. Just use them. • 7. The most essential: сейча́с, сего́дня, за́втра, вчера́, всегда́, никогда́, здесь, там, до́ма, хорошо́, пло́хо, бы́стро, ме́дленно.

topicos.explicacao: Consonant mutation in verbs, and a summary chart of the two conjugations in the present. Some verbs change the last consonant of the stem. In the second conjugation the change usually happens only in the я form (люблю́ but лю́бишь, лю́бят). In the first conjugation (for example писа́ть) the changed consonant stays in all forms (пишу́, пи́шешь, пи́шут). English has a faint echo of this ("office" and "officer", "electric" and "electricity", where k becomes s), but in Russian it is regular and predictable. topicos.titulo: The irregular verbs you will use most
topicos.explicacao: Few verbs break the rule, but they appear every day. Memorise these forms. Careful: the verb «есть» (to eat) is different from the «есть» of «У меня есть» (there is, exists): «Я ем суп» (I eat soup) × «У меня есть суп» (I have soup). «Идти» and «хотеть» appeared in earlier lessons.

A scene you have lived (or will). You already know how to conjugate verbs, use the past, the future and the accusative case. Now imagine another scene. You are in Russia. You want to say you are in your room. You think: "room in Russian is ко́мната. I'll say я в ко́мната." The person gives you a strange look and corrects you: — Я в ко́мнате. You look again. It is the same word, ко́мната. But now it ends in -е, not -а. You think: "Why? I already changed this word for the accusative (ко́мнату). Has it changed again? How many forms does this word have?" This happens to every Russian learner, and it happens because you have just met the prepositional case. It sounds like one more complicated case. It is not. Five minutes of careful reading and you will understand the little secret that solves everything. What is the prepositional case, and why is it called that? First, a question: why is this case called prepositional? Memorise this: the prepositional case is the only case in Russian that NEVER appears alone. It always comes after a preposition. That is where the name comes from: it is the case "of the preposition". It does not exist without one. Never, in any sentence, in any context. The nominative can appear alone (это дом), the accusative can appear alone (я вижу дом), but the prepositional always has a preposition before it. Always. And what is it for? Here is the answer: the prepositional case is used to say WHERE things are. It is the case of place. When you want to say "I am in the room", "I live in Russia", "the book is on the table", "I work at the factory", in all of these sentences the noun goes into the prepositional case. It is the "where" case. As simple as that. (It is also used with the preposition «о» to say what you are talking or thinking "about".) English puts all the meaning in the little words "in", "on", "at", and the noun never changes. Russian changes both the little word and the ending of the noun.

topicos.titulo: The little secret: open places and closed places
topicos.explicacao: The little secret: open places and closed places. Now comes the most charming part. Pay attention, because here is the key to everything. Russian has two main prepositions for "where": В and НА. Both can mean "in", "on" or "at". But Russian chooses between them with a very simple logic. В → for CLOSED places: places you can go inside, places with walls, doors, an interior. НА → for OPEN, WIDE places: places where you are on, on top of, on the surface. The magic test: ask yourself, can you go inside? YES → В (shop, room, cinema, theatre, house, school, factory, restaurant, museum...). NO, it is a wide, open place → НА (square, street, park, station, market, mountain, river...). Look at how it works. Комната (room): you can go inside → В. Магазин (shop): you can go inside → В. Площадь (square): wide, open → НА. Улица (street): open → НА. Работа (work): not a physical place but an activity → НА. Урок (lesson): not a place but an event → НА. Концерт (concert): not a place but an event → НА. The general rule: can you go inside? If yes, В. If it is wide, open, or an event or activity, НА. English does something similar, only less neatly: you are "in" the room but "on" the street, "at" the station, "at" a concert, "at" work. (A few words, like почта, break the logic. Learn them as exceptions.)

tabelas.titulo: The little secret: open places and closed places

topicos.titulo: The bridge with English: В = in, НА = on / at
topicos.explicacao: The bridge with English: В = in, НА = on / at. Here is the nicest thing: you already do this in English without noticing. You say: I am in the room. I am in the shop. I am in the cinema. I am on the square. I am on the street. I am at the station. English picks "in", "on" or "at" depending on the place, and sometimes it is hard to explain why (on the bus, in the car, at work). Russian does the same with just two words. The preposition В works like our "in". The preposition НА works like our "on / at", with a nuance of "on top of, on the surface". Compare. Notice that the preposition is a separate word, never merged into the noun. But the idea is the same as in English. You only have to choose between В (closed) and НА (open / event). And do not forget the second half: the noun changes its ending (комната → комнате).

tabelas.titulo: The bridge with English: В = in, НА = on / at

topicos.titulo: The 4 main prepositions of the prepositional case
topicos.explicacao: The 4 main prepositions of the prepositional case. The prepositional case is governed by four main prepositions. Let's meet each one. • 1. В (in, inside). Use: closed places you can go inside. Question: Где? (Where?) Examples follow. Spelling variant: ВО. Before words that begin with в or ф followed by another consonant, ВО is used instead of В. Why? Euphony. Russian does not like certain consonant clusters: «в Владивостоке» would sound bad, so an -о- is inserted to separate them. • 2. НА (on, at). Use: open, wide places, or events and activities. Question: Где? (Where?) Examples follow. Notice that на also appears with places that "make no sense" (почта, работа, урок, концерт). The logic is not only "open vs. closed": it also includes events, activities and surfaces. And there are historical exceptions, which we will see later. • 3. О (about, concerning). Use: to talk about something. Question: О ком? О чём? (About whom? About what?) Examples follow. Spelling variants: ОБ and ОБО. О goes before a consonant: о кни́ге, о рабо́те, о теа́тре. ОБ goes before a vowel: об Ива́не, об А́нне, об э́том, об о́сени. ОБО goes before мне, всём, всех and a few other words that start with a hard consonant cluster: обо мне, обо всём, обо льде. Why? Euphony again. «О Иване» would sound bad, and «о мне» too. So Russian inserts об or обо to keep the vowels and consonants apart. (You do this in English with "a" / "an": a book, an apple.) • 4. ПРИ (at, in the presence of, in the time of). Use: rare in daily life, but it appears in formal and historical contexts and in contexts of closeness. ПРИ has three meanings: • 1. Attached to, next to: при университе́те (attached to the university). • 2. In the presence of: при де́тях (in front of the children). • 3. In the time of: при царе́ (in the time of the tsar).

linhas.TRANSLATION: I am at the post office.
I am at the North Pole.
I am talking about the book.
In the time of Tsar Nicholas...
In the time of Peter I...
There is a library attached to the university.
Don't say that in front of the children.

topicos.titulo: в and на: choosing by the picture of the place
topicos.explicacao: Both mean «in / at / on», but Russian chooses by picture. «В» = inside a closed or bounded space: в доме, в комнате, в сумке, and also countries and cities (в России, в Москве). «На» = on a surface (на столе, на полу, на стене), in a place seen as open space (на улице, на площади, на море) or at an event or activity (на работе, на уроке, на концерте). The word after в/на goes into the prepositional case (-е, -и): в доме, на столе. Some short masculine nouns have a prepositional in -у when they answer «где?»: в шкафу, в саду, в лесу, на полу, на мосту.
topicos.comparacao: English also uses «in / on / at», but not in the same places: Russian says «на работе» (literally «on work») and «на уроке» (literally «on the lesson»). The choice between в and на depends on the picture of the place: inside, on top, open space or event.

A lesson is an event: на.

topicos.titulo: The scissors rule of the prepositional
topicos.explicacao: The scissors rule of the prepositional. Now the mechanics. How does the noun change when it goes into the prepositional? The scissors work as always: • 1. Find the nominative form (the dictionary word). • 2. Apply the prepositional ending, which depends on the gender and on the ending. • 3. Done. The noun is in the prepositional. Look at the endings in the table. Notice that the rule is almost always -Е. Only feminine nouns in -ь and nouns in -ия/-ие take -И (written -ИИ for those in -ия/-ие). And neuter nouns in -мя take -ЕНИ. Let's look at each case in detail.

tabelas.titulo: The scissors rule of the prepositional

linhas.EXAMPLE: стол → столе́, дом → до́ме, го́род → го́роде
ночь → но́чи, дверь → две́ри, тетра́дь → тетра́ди

topicos.explicacao: The MASCULINE in the prepositional. The masculine is the easiest: always -Е. It does not matter whether it ends in a consonant, in -й or in -ь. The ending is -Е. Masculine in a consonant: pay attention to the stress. стол → столе́ (the stress moves to the ending); дом → до́ме (the stress stays on the stem). There is no fixed rule. You need to listen and memorise. Masculine in -ь: notice that the -ь disappears and -е comes in. Always. Masculine in -й: notice that the -й disappears and -е comes in.

The FEMININE in the prepositional. The feminine is a little more complex, because it depends on the ending. Feminine in -а: notice that the -а disappears and -е comes in. Feminine in -я: the -я disappears and -е comes in. Feminine in -ь → ending -И. Here is the exception: a feminine noun in -ь gets -И, not -е. The -ь disappears and -и comes in. Always. Feminine in -ия → ending -ИИ. Words in -ия get -ии (two "i"s). The -я disappears and -ии comes in. (A few feminine nouns in -ь also move the stress: любовь → о любви́.)

topicos.titulo: The neuter and the master table of the prepositional
topicos.explicacao: The NEUTER in the prepositional. The neuter is the simplest. Two rules. Neuter in -о: notice that the -о becomes -е. Always. Neuter in -е: words in -е usually stay the same. But words in -ие (with an "i" before the "e") get -ии: упражне́ние → упражне́нии, зна́ние → зна́нии, зда́ние → зда́нии. Why? The same logic as -ия → -ии. Neuter in -мя → ending -ЕНИ. Neuter words ending in -мя get -ени. There are about 10 of them, and you already know them from lesson 11. They are neuter and end in -мя. In the prepositional they become -мени. The master table of the prepositional. Here is the table that solves everything.

tabelas.titulo: The master table of the prepositional

topicos.titulo: Where is it? лежать, стоять, сидеть, висеть
topicos.explicacao: In English we say «is» for everything: «the book is on the table». In Russian the verb chooses the position of the object: «лежать» (lying, horizontal), «стоять» (standing), «сидеть» (sitting), «висеть» (hanging). To sound natural, avoid «есть» and use the right verb: «Книга лежит на столе», «Лампа стоит на столе», «Кот сидит на диване», «Картина висит на стене». These verbs are 2nd conjugation: лежу, лежишь, лежит, лежим, лежите, лежат; сижу, сидишь...; стою, стоишь...; вишу, висишь...
topicos.comparacao: English uses «is» (or «sits», «hangs») for position, but Russian always says whether the object is lying, standing, sitting or hanging.

topicos.explicacao: The question "where?" versus "where to?". Here is one of the most important things in the whole lesson. Pay attention. Russian distinguishes between where (place) and where to (movement), and that distinction changes the case. ГДЕ? (Where?) → prepositional. You are already at the place. КУДА? (Where to?) → accusative. You are going to the place. English does the same with its little words: "in the room" (place) versus "into the room" or "to the room" (movement). Russian does it by changing the case after the same preposition. The rule: В + prepositional = "in / at" (where). В + accusative = "to / into" (where to). НА + prepositional = "on / at" (where). НА + accusative = "to / onto" (where to). It is the same preposition, but the case changes with the meaning. If it is a place, prepositional. If it is movement, accusative. Practical examples follow. That is all. The same preposition В or НА changes the case of the noun according to the meaning. Place → prepositional. Movement → accusative.

topicos.titulo: The exceptions: the irregular nouns in -У/-Ю
topicos.explicacao: The exceptions: the irregular nouns in -У/-Ю. Here is a point that is rarely explained well. A few masculine nouns take -У (or -Ю) in the prepositional, instead of -Е. But careful: only when the preposition is В or НА. With О, they go back to -Е. Look at the list of the most common irregular ones: the ending is -У (always stressed), and it only works with В and НА. Compare. The rule: when В/НА mean a place, these nouns use -У. When О means "about", they use the normal -Е. They have a split personality. Example sentences follow.

topicos.titulo: Support tables and common mistakes in the prepositional
topicos.explicacao: Support tables: adjectives, possessives, pronouns and transport in the prepositional. Pronouns with О (about): обо мне · о тебе́ · о нём · о ней · о нас · о вас · о них. Means of transport (НА + prepositional): е́хать на авто́бусе, на метро́, на маши́не, на по́езде, на такси́; лете́ть на самолёте. The mistakes English speakers WILL make in the prepositional. Mistake 1: using the accusative instead of the prepositional. ❌ Wrong: Я в ко́мнату (meaning "I am in the room"). ✅ Right: Я в ко́мнате. You learned the accusative first (lesson 14) and tend to use the accusative ending for everything. But "I am in the room" is place, not movement, so it is prepositional. Mistake 2: using no preposition at all. ❌ Wrong: Я ко́мнате. ✅ Right: Я в ко́мнате. The prepositional never appears alone. It always comes with a preposition (В, НА, О, ПРИ). Without a preposition there is no prepositional. Mistake 3: using В instead of НА (and vice versa). ❌ Wrong: Я в пло́щади. ✅ Right: Я на пло́щади. A square is an open place, so it takes НА. The rule of open versus closed places solves 90% of this. Mistake 4: forgetting that a feminine in -ь takes -И, not -Е. ❌ Wrong: Я в но́че. ✅ Right: Я в но́чи. Mistake 5: forgetting that -ия takes -ии. ❌ Wrong: Я в Росси́е. ✅ Right: Я в Росси́и. Mistake 6: using О when the next word begins with a vowel. ❌ Wrong: Я говорю́ о Ива́не. ✅ Right: Я говорю́ об Ива́не. Before a vowel, О becomes ОБ, for euphony (like English "a" versus "an"). Mistake 7: using ОБ instead of ОБО. ❌ Wrong: Я говорю́ об мне. ✅ Right: Я говорю́ обо мне. Before мне, всём, всех and a few other words that begin with a consonant cluster, use ОБО. Mistake 8: forgetting that -мя takes -ени. ❌ Wrong: Я в вре́мя. ✅ Right: Я во вре́мени. Words in -мя get -ени in the prepositional, and В becomes ВО before this word. Mistake 9: confusing "where" and "where to". ❌ Wrong: Я иду́ в ко́мнате (meaning "I am going into the room"). ✅ Right: Я иду́ в ко́мнату. "I am going into the room" is movement → accusative. "I am in the room" is place → prepositional. Mistake 10: using -у/-ю with О. ❌ Wrong: Я говорю́ о лесу́. ✅ Right: Я говорю́ о ле́се. The irregular nouns in -у/-ю only work with В/НА. With О they go back to -е.

topicos.titulo: Где? and Куда? with в and на; на + languages
topicos.explicacao: The choice between в and на continues with movement: if you use в with «где?», you also use в with «куда?» (в школе → в школу). If you use на, you use на in both (на работе → на работу). With movement the word goes into the accusative (-а becomes -у). English: «at school» and «to school»; Russian: only the ending changes. «На» is also used for languages: «Я говорю на русском языке», «Я читаю на английском».

topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: • 1. The prepositional is the only Russian case that always comes after a preposition. That is why it is called prepositional. STEP 2: • 2. It is used to say WHERE things are. It is the case of place. STEP 3: • 3. The two main prepositions are В and НА. Both mean "in / at / on". STEP 4: • 4. The little secret: В for closed places (you can go inside); НА for open places or events (square, street, class, work, concert). STEP 5: • 5. Think of В as "in": I am in the room → я в ко́мнате. STEP 6: • 6. The 4 prepositions: В (in), НА (on / at), О/ОБ/ОБО (about), ПРИ (at, attached to, in the time of). STEP 7: • 7. Prepositional endings: STEP 8: Masculine: -Е (always). STEP 9: Feminine in -а/-я: -Е. STEP 10: Feminine in -ь: -И. STEP 11: Feminine in -ия: -ИИ. STEP 12: Neuter in -о/-е: -Е. STEP 13: Neuter in -ие: -ИИ. STEP 14: Neuter in -мя: -ЕНИ. STEP 15: • 8. Where vs. where to: STEP 16: Где? (where) → prepositional (я в ко́мнате). STEP 17: Куда? (where to) → accusative (я иду́ в ко́мнату). STEP 18: • 9. topicos.aulaTitulo: Days of the week and clock time
topicos.explicacao: In Russian, the days of the week are written with a small letter, unlike English, where Monday, Tuesday and the rest always get a capital. To say "on Monday", use «в» + the day: «в понедельник». Days that end in -а change it to -у (the accusative): «в пятницу», «в субботу», «в среду». Before «вторник» you use «во»: «во вторник». «Воскресенье» does not change: «в воскресенье».
topicos.comparacao: in English we say "on Monday" or "on Mondays". In Russian the day takes only «в» and the accusative ending, and there is no capital letter.

erros.motivo: A day of the week does not take a capital letter in the middle of a sentence.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Days of the week and clock time
topicos.explicacao: To ask: «Который час?» or «Сколько времени?». To answer, «час» changes like «рубль»: 1 → «час»; 2, 3 and 4 → «часа»; 5 to 12 → «часов». For half hours, say «половина» + the NEXT hour in the genitive: 2:30 = «половина третьего» (literally "half of the third"). To say at what time something happens, use «в» + the hour: «в три часа», «в пять часов». «Один час» becomes simply «в час».
topicos.comparacao: in English we say "half past two", counting from the hour that has gone. Russian counts toward the hour that is coming: "half of the third". (British English "half two" works the same way as the Russian.)

topicos.titulo: Verbs with -ся: the action comes back to the doer
topicos.explicacao: Some verbs end in -ся, such as «просыпаться» (to wake up) and «умываться» (to wash oneself). The action comes back to the person who does it, like "to get oneself up". English often leaves this out ("I wash", "I wake up"), or uses "myself", but Russian marks it on the verb. Conjugate normally and add -сь if the form ends in a vowel (я просыпаюсь, вы просыпаетесь) or -ся if it ends in a consonant (он просыпается, они просыпаются). «Вставать» (to get up) follows the same pattern without -ся: я встаю.

exemplos.pt: I get up at seven o'clock.
We have lunch in a café.

topicos.explicacao: We have already seen «Где?» (where): «в» + prepositional («в магазине»). To ask «Куда?» (where to, with movement), use the ACCUSATIVE: «Я иду в магазин», «Я еду на работу». In short: standing still → prepositional; moving → accusative. For "home" there is a word of its own, with no preposition: «домой» (going home); "at home" is «дома». The verbs «идти» (on foot) and «ехать» (by bus, car or train) are irregular: learn the forms.
topicos.comparacao: in English we say "in the shop" for place and "to the shop" for movement. Russian keeps the same preposition and changes the ending of the word.

topicos.titulo: The past: the general idea and the "scissors"
topicos.explicacao: Before we start, an honest word about Russian. You already know how to conjugate verbs in the present. You know the scissors. You know the pronouns. You know the adverbs (вчера, сегодня, завтра). Now comes the final step: talking about what happened and what is going to happen. But first, an important point that is rarely said honestly: the Russian past you learn here is the past of actions in progress. It does not tell you that an action was finished and closed. It tells you that something was going on, was repeated, or lasted. It is the English "I was reading", "I used to work", "I lived" (without saying how it ended). Likewise, the Russian future you learn here is the future of an action that will go on or repeat, without a marked end: "I will be reading", "I will work", "I will live". This is fundamental for understanding what you are learning. You are not learning "the" past of Russian; you are learning one past, the one for actions in progress, repeated actions and actions without a marked end. Later, when you are ready, you will find another past and another future (the "completed" pair, which says "I read it through", "I will finish reading it"). That is for another time. For now, stay with this one. The good news: this past and this future are the most used in everyday speech. They are the basis of storytelling. With them you can already tell your life. Let's go. PART 1: THE PAST. The scissors rule for the past. You already know the scissors of the present: cut -ТЬ from the infinitive. You have the stem. Paste on the personal ending of the present. The past uses the same scissors with one difference: the past ending does not depend on the person. It depends on the gender. English is the opposite. In English the past form is the same for everyone ("I read, you read, she read"); Russian ignores the person but marks the gender. There are four past endings. That is all. Four endings. Nothing more.

tabelas.titulo: The scissors rule for the past

topicos.explicacao: The big difference in Russian. Here is the most important thing you need to understand: in the present, the verb agrees with the PERSON. In the past, the verb agrees with the GENDER of the subject. Compare. PRESENT (agrees with the person): Я чита́ю. (I read.) Ты чита́ешь. (You read.) Он чита́ет. (He reads.) Она́ чита́ет. (She reads.) Мы чита́ем. (We read.) PAST (agrees with the gender): Я чита́л. (I was reading, if I am a man.) Я чита́ла. (I was reading, if I am a woman.) Ты чита́л. (You were reading, if you are a man.) Ты чита́ла. (You were reading, if you are a woman.) Он чита́л. (He was reading: masculine.) Она́ чита́ла. (She was reading: feminine.) Оно́ чита́ло. (It was reading: neuter.) Мы чита́ли. (We were reading: any gender.) Вы чита́ли. (You were reading: any gender.) Они́ чита́ли. (They were reading: any gender.) Notice: in the singular, the ending changes with the gender. In the plural it is always -ЛИ, whatever the gender. This means that if you are a man and you say "I was reading", it is я чита́л. If you are a woman and you say "I was reading", it is я чита́ла. A man never says «я чита́ла». A woman never says «я чита́л». It is automatic: you do not think "I am a man, I will use -л". You simply use the form that matches you. (In English you only see a trace of this in pronouns: he/she. In Russian a woman talking about herself has to say it in the verb.)

The most common question: "if a man asks a woman, is it -Л or -ЛА?" Every learner has this doubt. Let's answer it clearly. There is one rule and it always holds: the past ending agrees with the GENDER OF THE SUBJECT, that is, of the person who does the action. It does not matter who asks, or who speaks. What matters is who is spoken about. Let me break it down with examples. Situation 1: a man asks a woman: — Ты чита́ла вчера́? (Were you reading yesterday?) The man is asking a woman. The woman is the subject of the sentence (she is the one who was reading), so the ending is -ЛА. The man used -ЛА because he is referring to her, not to himself. The woman answers: — Да, я чита́ла. (Yes, I was.) She answers with -ЛА because she is a woman. She agrees with herself. Situation 2: a woman asks a man: — Ты чита́л вчера́? (Were you reading yesterday?) The woman is asking a man. The man is the subject, so the ending is -Л. The woman used -Л because she is referring to him. The man answers: — Да, я чита́л. (Yes, I was.) He answers with -Л because he is a man. Situation 3: a man asks another man: — Ты чита́л вчера́? — Да, я чита́л. Both use -Л because both are men. Situation 4: a woman asks another woman: — Ты чита́ла вчера́? — Да, я чита́ла. Both use -ЛА because both are women. The rule in one sentence: the past ending does not belong to the speaker. It belongs to the subject of the sentence. If the subject is male, it is -Л. If the subject is female, it is -ЛА. No matter who asks, who answers, or the gender of the other person. More examples to fix it in your mind follow. Notice the last pair: a man talking about a woman uses -ЛА (the subject is she, a woman). A woman talking about a man uses -Л (the subject is he, a man). The gender of the speaker does not matter. What matters is the gender of the subject. Another example, with the verb быть: A man says: Я был до́ма. (I was at home.) A woman says: Я была́ до́ма. (I was at home.) A man asks a woman: Ты была́ до́ма? (Were you at home?) A woman asks a man: Ты был до́ма? (Were you at home?) Always the same logic: the ending follows the subject, not the speaker.

topicos.explicacao: In the present there is no "to be" in Russian («Я студент»). In the past it appears and changes with the gender and number of the SUBJECT: «был» (masculine), «была» (feminine), «было» (neuter), «были» (plural). The speaker counts too: a man says «Я был дома», a woman says «Я была дома». To say "I had", replace «есть» with «был/была/было/были» and agree with the thing you had: «У меня был брат», «У меня была сестра». The negative uses «не было» and the genitive: «У меня не было сестры». At this level we use the everyday past; the difference between the two aspects of the verb will come in a lesson of its own.
topicos.comparacao: in English "I was" is the same for a man and a woman. In Russian the verb changes with the gender of the speaker: «я был» (a man), «я была» (a woman).

exemplos.pt: I did not have a sister.

erros.motivo: In the past «есть» is not used: use был/была/было/были.

topicos.explicacao: Examples with regular verbs. Let's apply the scissors to eight regular verbs. Notice the translations: all of them describe an action in progress, repeated or lasting. ЧИТАТЬ (to read): stem ЧИТА-. ГОВОРИТЬ (to speak): stem ГОВОР-. РАБОТАТЬ (to work): stem РАБОТА-. ЖИТЬ (to live): stem ЖИ-. Attention: жить is irregular in the stress; in the feminine the stress goes to the end: жила́, not «жи́ла». ЗНАТЬ (to know): stem ЗНА-. ЛЮБИТЬ (to love): stem ЛЮБ-. СМОТРЕТЬ (to watch, look): stem СМОТРЕ-. ПИСАТЬ (to write): stem ПИСА-. English past forms ("read", "spoke", "worked") never change, but all these Russian forms do.

The most important irregular verbs. A few verbs do not follow the rule. Here are the main ones. БЫТЬ (to be): the most important. This is the verb you use when you want to say "I was at home" (Я был до́ма / Я была́ до́ма). ИДТИ (to go on foot): the most famous of the irregulars. Attention: the verb идти becomes шёл in the past. The stem is completely different, a linguistic fossil. Memorise it. МОЧЬ (can, to be able): мог, могла́, могло́, могли́. ЕСТЬ (to eat): ел, е́ла, е́ло, е́ли. ПИТЬ (to drink): пил, пила́, пи́ло, пи́ли. (English irregular verbs, like "go / went" and "eat / ate", are the same kind of fossil.)

topicos.titulo: Common mistakes and sentences in the past
topicos.explicacao: The mistakes English speakers WILL make in the past. Mistake 1: using the present, or looking for a person ending. ❌ Wrong: Я чита́ю вчера́. ✅ Right: Я чита́л вчера́. (a man) / Я чита́ла вчера́. (a woman). English speakers instinctively think "I read" and look for an "I" form of the past. It does not exist. The Russian past has no person. It has gender. Mistake 2: using -л for a woman. ❌ Wrong: Она́ чита́л вчера́. ✅ Right: Она́ чита́ла вчера́. If the subject is a woman, the ending is -ла, always. Mistake 3: using -л for a plural. ❌ Wrong: Они́ чита́л вчера́. ✅ Right: Они́ чита́ли вчера́. If the subject is plural, the ending is -ли, always, whatever the gender. Mistake 4: thinking that «я был» means "I am". ❌ Wrong: Я был брази́лец, meaning "I am Brazilian". ✅ Right: Я брази́лец (present, with no verb). Я был брази́лец (past: I was Brazilian). «Я был» means "I was". It never means "I am". For "I am", the verb does not appear: «я брази́лец». Mistake 5: not changing the form of быть for a woman. If you are a woman, never say «я был». Say «я была́». Always. Mistake 6: forgetting that идти becomes шёл. ❌ Wrong: Я идти́л вчера́. (It does not exist.) ✅ Right: Я шёл вчера́. (I was going yesterday.) The verb идти is irregular. The stem changes completely in the past. Mistake 7: using your own gender when you ask someone else. ❌ Wrong: A man asks a woman «Ты чита́л?» (using -л because he is a man). ✅ Right: A man asks a woman «Ты чита́ла?» (using -ла because she is a woman). This is the subtlest mistake. English speakers tend to use their own gender ending when asking a question, because in English the speaker's sex never affects the verb. But the ending follows the subject, not the person asking. If a man asks a woman, he uses -ла (because she is a woman). If a woman asks a man, she uses -л (because he is a man). Sentences in the past. Now real sentences, with adverbs of time. Notice the translations: all of them describe actions in progress or repeated. PART 2: THE FUTURE.

linhas.TRANSLATION: Yesterday I was reading a book. (a man)
Yesterday I was reading a book. (a woman)

topicos.explicacao: For the past of almost every verb, take the -ть off the infinitive and add -л (masculine), -ла (feminine), -ло (neuter) or -ли (plural): работать → работал, работала, работало, работали. The past does not change with the person (я, ты, он...), only with the gender and number of the subject. A man says «я читал», a woman says «я читала». Verbs in -ся keep the -ся: просыпался, просыпалась, просыпались. There are very common irregulars, such as «идти» → шёл, шла, шли.

erros.motivo: The past agrees with the gender of the person who does the action.
With «вчера» (yesterday) the verb goes into the past.

STEP 9: FUTURE: STEP 10: • 1. Conjugate быть in the future: бу́ду, бу́дешь, бу́дет, бу́дем, бу́дете, бу́дут. STEP 11: • 2. Paste on the infinitive of the main verb. STEP 12: • 3. Done. STEP 13: • 4. The main verb never changes. Never. STEP 14: • 5. The future has no gender. Я бу́ду чита́ть works for a man and a woman. STEP 15: • 6. Never say «бу́ду быть». Just «бу́ду». STEP 16: • 7. Negation: не before буду. Я не бу́ду чита́ть. STEP 17: THE THREE TENSES TOGETHER: STEP 18: Вчера́ я чита́л / чита́ла. (past, in progress) STEP 19: Сего́дня я чита́ю. (present) STEP 20: За́втра я бу́ду чита́ть. (future, in progress) STEP 21: That is it. You can now tell your life: what you were doing yesterday, what you do today, what you will be doing tomorrow.

topicos.titulo: Ordering food: the accusative in action
topicos.explicacao: When you order or say what you eat, the food goes into the accusative (the direct object). Only feminine words in -а change: -а becomes -у. Masculine and neuter nouns that are not living beings stay the same: «Я хочу рис», «Я хочу мясо», «Я хочу салат». English never marks this, so it is easy to forget: the word after the verb must change when it is feminine.

In Russian, many ideas of need and permission do not have a subject like "I". The person who needs goes into the dative (мне, тебе, ему...) and the word «нужно» comes after. After it can come an infinitive verb: «Мне нужно работать». If a noun follows, the form of «нужно» agrees with it: «нужен» (masculine), «нужна» (feminine), «нужно» (neuter), «нужны» (plural). But «можно» (it is allowed) and «нельзя» (it is not allowed) never change: they are adverbs.
topicos.comparacao: in English we say "I need water", with "I" as the subject. In Russian it is "to me is needed water" (Мне нужна вода), and «нужна» agrees with the water.

exemplos.pt: May I have some water, please?
You must not talk loudly here.

erros.motivo: The person who needs goes into the dative (мне); the thing needed agrees with «нужна».
