topicos.titulo: The 10 most common mistakes of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: These ten mistakes appear most often among English speakers. Fixing only these already makes your speech much more natural. Read each pair out loud: first the wrong one (to recognise the odd sound), then the right one (to fix it in memory).

erros.motivo: No «есть» in the present to say "is". (English forces you to say "it is"; Russian does not.)
The possessive agrees with the gender. (English "my" never changes.)
The direct object takes the accusative.
The double negative is compulsory in Russian.
The person who needs goes into the dative.
A question is made by intonation, with no «есть».

topicos.titulo: Verbal aspect: why verbs come in pairs
topicos.explicacao: A promise kept: why does almost every Russian verb come in a pair? In earlier lessons and vocabulary lists you noticed that almost all Russian verbs appear as a couple: де́лать / сде́лать (to do), чита́ть / прочита́ть (to read), писа́ть / написа́ть (to write), покупа́ть / купи́ть (to buy). The time has come to master this Russian superpower: verbal aspect (Вид глаго́ла). English has a dozen verb tenses ("I read", "I was reading", "I have read", "I had read"...). Russian has only three tenses (past, present and future), but it looks at any action through two different lenses. • 1. Imperfective (НСВ — Несоверше́нный вид) = THE FILM (process, routine, duration). It focuses on the action happening, repeating every day or lasting for a while, whether or not it finished. It corresponds to our "I was reading / I used to read / I read every day". • 2. Perfective (СВ — Соверше́нный вид) = THE PHOTOGRAPH (a single, completed result). It focuses on the end point, the mission accomplished, the finished result of one single occasion. It corresponds to our "I read the whole book / I have written the letter / I bought the ticket". The Compass: imperfective (НСВ) versus perfective (СВ). The big trick of the simple future (perfective): the perfective verb (сде́лать, прочита́ть, написа́ть, купи́ть) has no present. So when you apply the present-tense scissors to it, the result means COMPLETED FUTURE (and it never uses бу́ду!). де́лать (НСВ): я де́лаю (I do / am doing now) · я бу́ду де́лать (I will be doing / working on it). сде́лать (СВ): я сде́лаю (I will do it / I will get it done!) · ты сде́лаешь · он сде́лает.

linhas.1. IMPERFECTIVE (НСВ): THE FILM (ЧИТА́ТЬ: Process / duration (for two hours, all day). Repetition / habit (always, every day, often). The general fact ("Have you ever read Tolstoy?")
linhas.2. PERFECTIVE (СВ): THE PHOTOGRAPH (ПРОЧ: Completed result ("Done, I finished!"). A single, momentary action (once, suddenly). A sequence of events ("I woke up, had breakfast and left").

linhas.1. IMPERFECTIVE (НСВ): THE FILM (ЧИТА́ТЬ: всегда́ (always) · ча́сто (often) · обы́чно (usually) · ка́ждый день (every day) · до́лго (for a long time) · весь день (all day)
linhas.2. PERFECTIVE (СВ): THE PHOTOGRAPH (ПРОЧ: уже́ (already) · наконе́ц (finally) · вдруг (suddenly) · сра́зу (immediately) · весь / всю / всё (all, the whole)

linhas.1. IMPERFECTIVE (НСВ): THE FILM (ЧИТА́ТЬ: It exists! (Я чита́ю кни́гу сейча́с. I am reading a book now.)
linhas.2. PERFECTIVE (СВ): THE PHOTOGRAPH (ПРОЧ: IT DOES NOT EXIST! (Nobody completes something in the middle of "now"!)

linhas.1. IMPERFECTIVE (НСВ): THE FILM (ЧИТА́ТЬ: Вчера́ я чита́л кни́гу два часа́. (Yesterday I spent two hours reading a book: process.)
linhas.2. PERFECTIVE (СВ): THE PHOTOGRAPH (ПРОЧ: Вчера́ я прочита́л всю кни́гу! (Yesterday I read the whole book: completed!)

linhas.1. IMPERFECTIVE (НСВ): THE FILM (ЧИТА́ТЬ: Compound future (бу́ду + НСВ infinitive): За́втра я бу́ду чита́ть. (I will read / I will be reading.)
linhas.2. PERFECTIVE (СВ): THE PHOTOGRAPH (ПРОЧ: Simple future (conjugate the СВ verb!): За́втра я прочита́ю э́ту статью́! (I will read it through!)

topicos.explicacao: In Russian, almost every verb has TWO infinitives, called aspects. The imperfective looks at the action as a process, habit or repetition: «Я читал книгу» = I was reading a book (perhaps without finishing it). The perfective looks at the action as a whole, completed, with a result: «Я прочитал книгу» = I read the book to the end. English shows the same idea in the difference between "I was reading" and "I read it through" / "I finished reading". Guiding question: does the process or habit matter (imperfective), or the completed result (perfective)? The perfective is conjugated like any verb (1st or 2nd conjugation) and is often formed with a PREFIX: делать → сделать. Attention: the perfective has no present tense; its present-looking forms mean the future (next lesson). So when you study a verb, always study the pair: imperfective / perfective.
topicos.comparacao: English uses different tenses or extra words for the same verb ("was reading" versus "read through"). Russian uses two different verbs, almost always similar to each other.

exemplos.pt: Yesterday I was reading a book.
Yesterday I read the book (to the end).
Every day I used to read (habit).

erros.motivo: Habit and repetition call for the imperfective.

topicos.titulo: Clue words for choosing the aspect
topicos.explicacao: Certain words point to the aspect. Imperfective: каждый день, всегда, часто, редко, иногда, обычно, долго, весь день (habit, repetition or duration). Perfective: уже, сразу, наконец, за час (result, deadline, a single completed action). Test question: «Что ты делал вчера?» (imperfective: what were you doing?) versus «Что ты сделал вчера?» (perfective: what did you do, what did you get done?).

exemplos.pt: What did you do (get done) yesterday?

topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The 20 most important aspect pairs (A2). Learn each verb as a pair: imperfective (the film) and perfective (the photograph). In the perfective column, the forms in brackets are the simple future (я / они), which is how the perfective is conjugated. STEP 2: Summary chart: verbal aspect (НСВ versus СВ). The pairs are formed in three ways: 1. adding a prefix; 2. changing an inner suffix (-ать/-ять ↔ -ить/-нуть and similar); 3. using a different root altogether (the royal trio говорить / сказать, брать / взять, класть / положить).

tabelas.titulo: 1. Adding a prefix (с-, про-, на-, по-, вы-, при-)

linhas.TRANSLATION: to prepare / cook · to have lunch
to drink · to eat · to learn by heart

tabelas.titulo: 2. Changing the inner suffix (-ать/-ять ↔ -ить/-нуть and similar)

linhas.TRANSLATION: to understand · to rest · to give

topicos.explicacao: The most common way to form the perfective is to add a prefix to the imperfective. The most frequent ones: с- (делать → сделать), про- (читать → прочитать), на- (писать → написать), по- (смотреть → посмотреть), при- (готовить → приготовить), вы- (учить → выучить), у- (видеть → увидеть). Other pairs change the ending: покупать → купить, отвечать → ответить. Once formed, the perfective is conjugated like any verb; in the past: прочитал, прочитала, прочитали.

In English the future is made with "will" ("I will read") or "going to" ("I'm going to read"). Russian has TWO forms of the future, depending on the aspect. The first is the compound future, of the imperfective: «буду» + imperfective infinitive = I will do / I will be doing (process, habit, duration). The verb «быть» in the future: я буду, ты будешь, он будет, мы будем, вы будете, они будут. The verb that follows always stays in the infinitive.
topicos.comparacao: English says "I will read", which looks a lot like this: «буду» works like "will be", followed by the infinitive. «Буду читать» is like "I will be reading" (for a while, regularly).

erros.motivo: «Буду» is not used with a perfective verb.

topicos.explicacao: The perfective is conjugated with the same endings as the present (1st or 2nd conjugation), but the meaning is FUTURE: the action has not been done yet and will be completed. Прочитать → я прочитаю, ты прочитаешь, он прочитает, мы прочитаем, вы прочитаете, они прочитают. Verbs with a prefix follow the pattern of the base verb: писать → напишу (с → ш), смотреть → посмотрю. Some pairs change the root and the consonant mutates: купить → куплю (п → пл), ответить → отвечу (т → ч), сказать → скажу. And «дать» is irregular: дам, дашь, даст, дадим, дадите, дадут. «Буду» is never used with the perfective.
topicos.comparacao: in English the future of a completed action is "I will read it" or "I'll finish reading it". Russian uses the perfective, conjugated as if it were the present.

exemplos.pt: Tomorrow I will read the book (to the end).

topicos.titulo: буду versus perfective: process or result
topicos.explicacao: The choice follows the same logic as in the past. Do you want to talk about a process, a habit or a duration? Use «буду» + imperfective infinitive. Do you want to talk about a result, a single completed action? Use the perfective future.

tabela.exemplo: Завтра я буду работать весь день.

topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: FUTURE: two forms, depending on the aspect. STEP 2: • 1. Imperfective future (process, habit, duration): conjugate быть: бу́ду, бу́дешь, бу́дет, бу́дем, бу́дете, бу́дут. STEP 3: • 2. Paste on the imperfective infinitive of the main verb: Я бу́ду чита́ть. STEP 4: • 3. The main verb never changes. Never. STEP 5: • 4. The future has no gender: Я бу́ду чита́ть works for a man and a woman. STEP 6: • 5. Perfective future (a completed result): conjugate the perfective verb with the present-tense endings: Я прочита́ю, ты прочита́ешь, они прочита́ют. STEP 7: • 6. Never mix «бу́ду» with a perfective verb, and never say «бу́ду быть». Just «бу́ду». STEP 8: • 7. Negation: не before the verb: Я не бу́ду чита́ть. Я не прочита́ю. STEP 9: • 8. Quick test: process, habit, duration → бу́ду + imperfective; one completed result → perfective. STEP 10: THE THREE TENSES TOGETHER: STEP 11: Вчера́ я чита́л / чита́ла. (past, in progress) STEP 12: Сего́дня я чита́ю. (present) STEP 13: За́втра я бу́ду чита́ть. (future, in progress) STEP 14: За́втра я прочита́ю кни́гу. (future, completed) STEP 15: That is it. You can now tell your life: what you were doing yesterday, what you do today, and what you will do tomorrow.

In English "go" does everything (and you add "on foot" or "by bus" if you need to). In Russian, verbs of motion come in TWO verbs for each idea. The determinate verb describes an action that is happening now, in a single direction: «идти», «ехать». The indeterminate verb describes a habit, a round trip or an ability: «ходить», «ездить». On top of that, Russian separates the MEANS: on foot (идти / ходить) versus by transport (ехать / ездить). Guiding question: am I going now, in one direction (идти / ехать)? Or is it a habit, a round trip or an ability (ходить / ездить)? In the past, «ходил» can mean "went and came back". With means of transport you use «на» + prepositional: на автобусе, на метро, на машине.
topicos.comparacao: in English the same "go" serves for walking, for the bus, for now or for every day ("I go to work by bus"). Russian chooses the verb by the means and by the situation.

exemplos.pt: I am walking to the shop (now).

exemplos.ru: Я хожу в магазин каждый день.
exemplos.pt: I go to the shop every day (habit).
He is on his way to work (now).

exemplos.ru: Он ездит на работу на автобусе.
exemplos.pt: He goes to work by bus (always).

erros.errado: Я иду на работу на автобусе.
erros.certo: Я еду на работу на автобусе.

erros.errado: Я иду в магазин каждый день.
erros.certo: Я хожу в магазин каждый день.
erros.motivo: A habit calls for the indeterminate: ходить.

topicos.titulo: Verbs of motion: two questions, the table of the 4 verbs and the prefixes
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The two questions Russian asks before saying "to go". In English the verb "go" does it all: "I go to the baker's on foot", "I'm flying to Moscow", "I'm going to work now" and "I go to work every day". In Russian you can never use one verb for those four sentences! Before speaking, Russian asks two questions. • 1. Question 1: ON FOOT or BY VEHICLE? If you use your own legs, you use the pair ИДТИ́ / ХОДИ́ТЬ. If wheels, rails, a boat or a plane are involved (even to another city or country!), you must use the pair Е́ХАТЬ / Е́ЗДИТЬ. • 2. Question 2: ONE DIRECTION NOW (an arrow →) or ROUND TRIP / HABIT (⇄)? One-way (→ ИДТИ́ / Е́ХАТЬ): you are moving in a single direction toward a specific destination (now or in a specific plan). Multi-directional (⇄ ХОДИ́ТЬ / Е́ЗДИТЬ): repeated movement (a round-trip routine: every day, often), movement with no fixed direction (strolling around town) or, in the past, a completed round trip (Вчера́ я ходи́л в кино́ = Yesterday I went to the cinema and I am already back!). STEP 2: The master table of the 4 verbs of motion. The golden secret of the past: in Russian, saying Вчера́ я ходи́л(а) в музе́й (on foot) or В про́шлом году́ мы е́здили в Росси́ю (by vehicle or plane) is exactly the same as saying Вчера́ я был(а́) в музе́е / Мы бы́ли в Росси́и: you went there and you are already back! STEP 3: The 5 spatial prefixes of motion (ПО-, ПРИ-, У-, В-, ВЫ-). When we put a spatial prefix in front of the verbs of motion, we show the exact direction of the action. STEP 4: Summary chart: verbs of motion.

tabelas.titulo: The master table of the 4 verbs of motion

linhas.1. ИДТИ́ (→) ON FOOT, ONE DIRECTION NOW: шёл, шла, шли (was on the way)
linhas.2. ХОДИТЬ (⇄) ON FOOT, ROUTINE / ROUND T: ходи́л, ходи́ла, ходи́ли (went and came back = был!)
linhas.3. Е́ХАТЬ (→) BY VEHICLE, ONE DIRECTION: е́хал, е́хала, е́хали (was travelling on the way)
linhas.4. Е́ЗДИТЬ (⇄) BY VEHICLE, ROUTINE / ROU: е́здил, е́здила, е́здили (travelled and came back = был!)

tabelas.titulo: The 5 spatial prefixes of motion (ПО-, ПРИ-, У-, В-, ВЫ-)

linhas.PREFIX AND MEANING: 1. ПО- (set off / go, in the future): start of movement or the future
linhas.KEY EXAMPLES (WITH PREPOSITION + CASE!): За́втра я пойду́ в кино́ (Tomorrow I will go to the cinema). Ле́том мы пое́дем в Москву́ (In the summer we will go to Moscow).
Во ско́лько ты придёшь домо́й? (What time will you get home?) Он прие́хал из Брази́лии в Росси́ю. (He came from Brazil to Russia.)
Анна уже́ ушла́ с рабо́ты (Anna has already left work). Он уе́хал из го́рода (He left the city).
Мо́жно войти́ в ко́мнату? (May I come into the room?)

linhas.PREFIX AND MEANING: 5. ВЫ- (go out, for a short time or to get off)
linhas.ON FOOT (IMPERFECTIVE / PERFECTIVE): выходи́ть / вы́йти (вы́йду, вы́шел; the stress is always on вы-)
linhas.KEY EXAMPLES (WITH PREPOSITION + CASE!): Дире́ктор вы́шел на пять мину́т (The director stepped out for five minutes and will be back!). Я выхожу́ на сле́дующей остано́вке (I get off at the next stop).

topicos.titulo: Direction prefixes and the future with по-
topicos.explicacao: Motion verbs take prefixes that show direction: при- (arrive), у- (leave, go away), в- (go in), вы- (go out). On foot: приходить, уходить, входить, выходить. By vehicle: приезжать, уезжать, въезжать, выезжать. The prefix «по-» makes the perfective of «идти» and «ехать»: «пойти» and «поехать». They are used for the future («Завтра я пойду в магазин» = tomorrow I will go to the shop) and to say that someone has set off («Я поехал на работу» = I have left for work). Past tense: пошёл, пошла, пошли; поехал, поехала, поехали.

erros.motivo: For the future use «по-» + a conjugated form (пойду), never the bare infinitive.

erros.errado: Я прихожу на работу на автобусе.
erros.certo: Я приезжаю на работу на автобусе.
erros.motivo: With a vehicle use «приезжать» (приходить is on foot).

topicos.explicacao: Picture a scene you will probably live. You are in Russia and you are cold. You want to say "I am cold". You think: "cold in Russian is хо́лодно, so I will say я хо́лодно." The person gives you a puzzled look and corrects you: — Мне хо́лодно. You stare. A new word, мне, that you have never seen. You wonder: "Why can't I just say я хо́лодно?" And the person explains: — Because the cold is not yours. The cold happens to you. That is the doorway into the dative case, and it shows one of the most beautiful ideas in Russian. Pay attention: after this lesson you will see the language with new eyes.

topicos.titulo: What is the dative case? (the idea behind the grammar)
topicos.explicacao: What is the dative case? Before any table, one question. In English grammar, the dative is the case of the "indirect object". It is the case of "to" and "for": "I gave the book to Ivan." "I spoke to Maria." "I bought a present for you." The dative belongs to the one who receives the action, not the one who does it. But that definition is dry. Here is the one that changes everything: the dative is the case of things that happen TO US but are not OURS. Think about it. Heat. Cold. Hunger. Thirst. Pleasure. Displeasure. Liking. Needing. Hurting. All of these happen to us, but we do not do them. They come from outside and reach us. In English we say: I am hot. I am cold. I like coffee. I need help. I feel pain. Notice that every sentence starts with I, as if the heat, the cold, the liking, the need and the pain were things we own. But they are not. The heat is not yours; it happens to you. The cold is not yours; it happens to you. The coffee pleases you. Help is missing for you. Russian captures this precisely, and all of these go into the dative. Look: the "I" disappears and мне comes in. The verb "to be" also disappears (you know that from Lesson 4). The sentence becomes: "To me — hot." "To me — cold." "To me — pleasing is the coffee." It is a mental revolution: Russian does not say that you are hot, it says that it is hot to you. English has a faint echo of this: "it seems to me", "it is all the same to me", "it occurs to me". Russian does it for dozens of everyday ideas.

tabelas.titulo: What is the dative case? (the idea behind the grammar)

linhas.RUSSIAN: Мне нра́вится ко́фе. (To me the coffee is pleasing.)
Мне нужна́ по́мощь. (To me help [is] necessary.)
Мне два́дцать лет. (To me [are] twenty years.)

topicos.titulo: The dative: "to me" and the pronouns
topicos.explicacao: The dative is the case of "to me, for me". Before the deep idea, let us be practical. In its simplest form the dative is the case of "to" and "for" someone: the receiver. To me — мне. For me — мне. I gave the book to Ivan — я дал кни́гу Ива́ну. I spoke to Maria — я сказа́л Мари́и. I bought a present for you — я купи́л пода́рок тебе́. These are the most obvious uses. If you understood the accusative (the case of the action) and the prepositional (the case of place), the dative is the case of the recipient: the one who receives something. But the dative is much more than that. It is also the case of: physical states (cold, heat, hunger, thirst); emotional states (sad, glad, bad, well); liking (нра́виться); needing (ну́жно, нужна́); age (мне 20 лет); verbs such as help, phone, tell, write (to someone). All of this is dative, because all of it is something that happens to you, not something you do. First step: the personal pronouns in the dative. They are the foundation; without them you will not get far. Here they are. Notice: мне (to me) looks like меня́ (accusative), but with -е instead of -я. тебе́ (to you) looks like тебя́ (accusative), but with -е. ему́ and ей (to him, to her) are forms of their own, and нам / вам / им are short and easy to memorise. How to use them: learn them like magic words. They will appear in almost every sentence you build.

tabelas.titulo: Personal pronouns in the dative (first step)

linhas.TRANSLATION: to you, for you (plural or formal)

topicos.titulo: The big distinction: what YOU DO vs. what HAPPENS to you
topicos.explicacao: This is the most important idea of the lesson. Russian has two ways of linking a person and a thing: STEP 1: the person DOES an action. The verb is active, the person is the subject and the thing is the object (accusative). STEP 2: a thing HAPPENS to the person. The verb is impersonal or describes a feeling, and the person is in the dative. Compare. What YOU DO (accusative) versus what HAPPENS to you (dative). Notice: in the first list I am the subject. I do the action: I love, I read, I see. In the second list the thing happens to me: the cold happens to me, the coffee pleases me, the need comes to me, the years are counted to me. Russian separates the two firmly. English speakers always start with "I": "I am cold." "I like coffee." "I am 20." Russian answers: "No. It is not yours. It happens to you. Use the dative."

linhas.TRANSLATION: To me it is cold. (I am cold.)
To me it is hot. (I am hot.)
To me it feels like eating. (I am hungry.)
To me the coffee is pleasing. (I like coffee.)
To me it is necessary to work. (I need to work.)
To me [are] twenty years. (I am 20 years old.)

topicos.explicacao: Here is a small secret nobody tells you. In English we say "I am hot" or "I have a headache", as if the heat or the pain were something we carry, a temporary possession. But the heat belongs to the room. It happens to you. You do not carry it; it wraps around you and arrives without being asked. Russian understands this. So in Russian you do not say "I am hot". You say: Мне жа́рко. (To me [it is] hot.) The heat is not mine; it happens to me. The "I" is not the subject but the dative. Try the test with other sensations: in Russian they all go into the dative, because they are things that happen to you, not things you own. Notice that the pattern is always мне + a word. The word can be an adverb (хо́лодно, жа́рко, пло́хо, хорошо́) or a verb (хо́чется). But мне is always there. This is one of the most used constructions in Russian. Every day you will say "мне хо́лодно" a thousand times, and "мне жа́рко", and "мне ну́жно". You are not "doing" the cold; you are "having" it, in the dative.

linhas.LITERAL TRANSLATION: To me it feels like eating.
To me it feels like drinking.
To me it feels like sleeping.

topicos.explicacao: The dative answers «кому? чему?» (to whom? to what?). In English we use "to" or "for" + someone: "I give the book to my brother." In Russian the word changes its ending. Singular, masculine and neuter: consonant + -у (брат → брату); -й and -ь become -ю (учитель → учителю); -о becomes -у (окно → окну); -е becomes -ю (море → морю). Feminine: -а and -я become -е (мама → маме, неделя → неделе); -ия becomes -ии (Мария → Марии); -ь becomes -и (ночь → ночи). Plural, for all genders: -ам or -ям (студенты → студентам, друзья → друзьям). Irregular: дочь → дочери, мать → матери.
topicos.comparacao: in English only a few pronouns change ("he/him", "we/us"). In Russian every noun and adjective changes its ending according to the case.

erros.motivo: «звонить» takes the dative (in English you just "phone her", but in Russian it is "phone to her").
The one who receives goes into the dative.

topicos.titulo: The big distinction: LIKING vs. LOVING
topicos.explicacao: This is the most charming part of Russian, and English hides it. In English we use "love" and "like" as the same thing at two strengths: I love Maria (intense). I like coffee (milder). Both are normal active verbs with "I" as the subject. Russian splits them by structure. ЛЮБИТЬ — to love (I do the action). Люби́ть works like "love": the subject is the person, the object is in the accusative. Notice that люби́ть takes the accusative (Мари́ю, кни́гу, жену́, роди́ну). Love is an action that leaves you. You are the agent. НРАВИТЬСЯ — to be pleasing, to like (the thing comes to you). Нра́виться works differently. Russian does not say "I like coffee". It says: Мне нра́вится ко́фе. (To me the coffee is pleasing.) Мне is the dative (to me). нра́вится is the verb (is pleasing). ко́фе is the SUBJECT of the sentence. In Russian the coffee is the one acting; it pleases me. Pleasure travels from the coffee to me, and I am in the dative because it happens to me. English has the same pattern in "the coffee appeals to me" or "that idea pleases me". Two important points: STEP 1: the verb agrees with the thing, not the person. Мне нра́вится ко́фе (singular, because ко́фе is singular). Мне нра́вятся кни́ги (plural, because кни́ги is plural). The person is always мне, ему́, ей, and so on. STEP 2: do not confuse it with люби́ть. The difference in one line: люби́ть, love leaves you, you are the agent, the thing is the object, accusative. Нра́виться, pleasure comes to you, the thing is the agent, you are the receiver, dative. Which to use? If it is a deep, active feeling of yours, люби́ть. If it is something that pleases you, gives you enjoyment, comes from outside, нра́виться. In general: люби́ть is for people (romantic, family love), for one's homeland and for much-loved things. Нра́виться is for food, music, films, cities, things that give pleasure. It also works for people, when the feeling is milder than love. Russian makes you think about where the feeling comes from: love leaves you, pleasure comes to you. Two different things, two verbs, two cases.

linhas.LITERAL TRANSLATION: To me the coffee is pleasing.
To me this book is pleasing.

linhas.WHAT HAPPENS: The love leaves me and goes to her.

linhas.TRANSLATION: Maria is pleasing to me / I like Maria.
linhas.WHAT HAPPENS: The pleasure comes from her to me.
My love for the book is active.

linhas.TRANSLATION: This book is pleasing to me.
linhas.WHAT HAPPENS: The pleasure comes from the book to me.

linhas.TRANSLATION: You are pleasing to me. (I like you, but less intense.)
I love the Russian language. (deep feeling)
I like the Russian language. (the pleasure of learning it)

topicos.titulo: Other uses of the dative: need, may, suit, phone
topicos.explicacao: Besides the "philosophical" uses, the dative has very practical ones. Here are the main ones. НУЖНО / НУЖНА́ / НУ́ЖНЫ — to need. In English: "I need something". In Russian: "to me [is] necessary something". The form of ну́жно agrees with the thing needed, not with the person: ну́жно when a verb follows (ну́жно рабо́тать); ну́жен when the noun is masculine; нужна́ when it is feminine; ну́жно when it is neuter; ну́жны when it is plural. The person is always in the dative: Мне ну́жно means "to me [it is] necessary". The need happens to you. НА́ДО — to need (a synonym of ну́жно). На́до works like ну́жно but is more colloquial. МО́ЖНО / НЕЛЬЗЯ́ — may / may not. Мо́жно means "it is possible, it is allowed". Нельзя́ means "it is not possible, it is not allowed". Both take the dative when the person is named. ВОЗМО́ЖНО — possible. Возмо́жно also goes with the dative. The verb НРА́ВИТЬСЯ (seen above): after "to need", it is the most common dative verb. ИДТИ́ — to suit, to look good on. Verbs of communication: помогать, звонить, писать, говорить, давать and so on. All of them put the recipient in the dative. Notice that all these verbs have a recipient, someone who receives the action, and that person goes into the dative. AGE: мне 20 лет. In English: "I am 20". In Russian: "to me [are] 20 years". The logic: age happens to you; you do not own the years. Dative.

linhas.TRANSLATION: I need a dictionary. (слова́рь is masculine)
May I come in? (Is it allowed to me to enter?)
He may. (It is allowed to him.)
It is possible for me to go.

topicos.titulo: Verbs and prepositions that take the dative
topicos.explicacao: Some verbs take the dative even when the English object looks direct: «звонить кому?» (to phone someone), «помогать кому?» (to help someone), «отвечать кому?» (to answer someone), «советовать кому?» (to advise someone). The verb «нравиться» flips the sentence: the person who likes goes into the dative and the thing liked is the subject: «Мне нравится музыка» (the music is pleasing to me). If the thing is plural, the verb is plural too: «Мне нравятся фильмы». The prepositions «к» (towards a person or place: «Я иду к другу») and «по» («по телефону», «по субботам») take the dative.

erros.motivo: The verb agrees with the thing that is liked.
To go to see a person, use «к» + dative.

tabela.question: кому?
tabela.exemplo: Мне нравится музыка. Мне нравятся фильмы.

topicos.titulo: Nouns in the dative and the master table
topicos.explicacao: Nouns in the dative (endings). Now the nouns. How do they change in the dative? The method is the same as always: STEP 1: find the nominative form (the dictionary form). STEP 2: add the dative ending, which depends on the gender and on the ending of the word. STEP 3: done. The dative endings are in the tables below. Notice: masculine (consonant, -й, -ь) takes -У/-Ю. Feminine in -а/-я takes -Е. Feminine in -ь and -ия takes -И/-ИИ. Neuter in -о/-е takes -У/-Ю. Neuter in -мя takes -ЕНИ. The big difference between the dative and the prepositional: masculine and neuter in -о/-е take -У/-Ю, not -Е. Compare. In the masculine and in the neuter in -о, the dative differs from the prepositional. In the feminine, they are the same. Then comes the master table of the dative, which solves everything.

linhas.EXAMPLE: друг → дру́гу, дом → до́му, стол → столу́

tabelas.titulo: The master table of the dative

topicos.titulo: Support tables and the prepositions к and по
topicos.explicacao: Support tables: plural, adjectives, possessives and the prepositions К and ПО with the dative. Prepositions of the dative: К (КО) = movement towards a person, or a doctor (идти́ к врачу́ = go to the doctor, е́хать к дру́гу = drive to a friend's, ко мне = to my place). ПО = along, by means of, on a subject (гуля́ть по у́лице / по го́роду = walk along the street / around the city, говори́ть по телефо́ну = talk on the phone, кни́га по исто́рии = a book on history). The big difference of the dative: it does two jobs. STEP 1: indirect object (to whom you give, speak, write). STEP 2: logical subject (in impersonal constructions). Notice that it is the same form but a different function. In the first example the dative is the recipient of the action. In the others the dative is the person who experiences a state. That is why the dative matters so much: it appears in two very common types of sentence. Normal sentences with an indirect object: я даю́ ему́ кни́гу. Impersonal sentences: мне хо́лодно, мне нра́вится. Without the dative you can say neither.

tabelas.titulo: Support tables: plural, adjectives, possessives and К / ПО with the dative
The two jobs of the dative

linhas.FUNCTION OF THE DATIVE: logical subject (to whom the cold happens)
logical subject (to whom the coffee is pleasing)
logical subject (to whom it is necessary)

topicos.explicacao: The mistakes English speakers WILL make with the dative. Mistake 1: using the nominative instead of the dative in impersonal constructions. Wrong: Я хо́лодно. Right: Мне хо́лодно. You think "I am cold" and translate word for word into «я хо́лодно». But Russian says «мне хо́лодно»: the I turns into мне (dative). Mistake 2: using the accusative instead of the dative with verbs of communication. Wrong: Я помога́ю его́. Right: Я помога́ю ему́. Помога́ть and other verbs of communication take the dative, not the accusative. In English "help him" looks like a plain object, so this one catches everyone. Verbs that take the dative: помога́ть (help), звони́ть (phone), писа́ть (write to someone), говори́ть (speak to someone), дава́ть (give to someone), расска́зывать (tell someone), улыба́ться (smile at someone), ве́рить (believe someone), меша́ть (disturb someone), зави́довать (envy someone), отвеча́ть (answer someone), дари́ть (give a present to someone), покупа́ть (buy for someone). Mistake 3: using the person as the subject of нра́виться. Wrong: Я нра́влюсь ко́фе. Right: Мне нра́вится ко́фе. Нра́виться is a special verb. It does not go with я; it goes with мне (dative). The subject is the thing, not the person. Ко́фе is the subject, мне is the one it pleases. Mistake 4: mixing up нра́виться and люби́ть. Wrong: Я нра́влю ко́фе. Right: Мне нра́вится ко́фе. (I like coffee.) Люби́ть = to love (an active feeling). Нра́виться = to be pleasing (pleasure that comes from outside). Different verbs with different structures. Mistake 5: using the nominative instead of the dative with ну́жно. Wrong: Я ну́жно рабо́тать. Right: Мне ну́жно рабо́тать. Ну́жно works like «мне хо́лодно»: the person goes into the dative, and the thing that is needed goes into the nominative. Mistake 6: using the wrong noun ending. Wrong: Я помога́ю Мари́я. Right: Я помога́ю Мари́и. Feminine in -ия takes -ии in the dative: Мари́я → Мари́и. Wrong: Я помога́ю друг. Right: Я помога́ю дру́гу. A masculine in a consonant takes -у in the dative. Mistake 7: forgetting that with нра́виться the verb agrees with the thing, not the person. Wrong: Мне нра́вится кни́ги. Right: Мне нра́вятся кни́ги. Кни́ги is plural, so the verb is plural: нра́вятся. Wrong: Мне нра́вятся ко́фе. Right: Мне нра́вится ко́фе. Ко́фе is singular, so the verb stays singular: нра́вится. Mistake 8: building the feeling with a preposition, as English does with "with" or "have". English says "I have a cold" or "I feel the cold". In Russian there is no preposition and no verb "have": just dative + word, мне хо́лодно. Mistake 9: putting «thank you» into the dative. In Russian "thank you" is simply спаси́бо, with no dative. (There is a formal construction благодарю́ вас / благодарю́ тебя́, where the verb благодари́ть takes the accusative.) Mistake 10: forgetting that нужно agrees with the thing needed. Wrong: Мне ну́жно по́мощь. Right: Мне нужна́ по́мощь. По́мощь is feminine, so нужна́, not ну́жно.

topicos.titulo: Age, feelings and need with the dative
topicos.explicacao: In Russian, age, feelings and need are said with the dative of the person, with no verb like «to have» or «to be»: «Мне 20 лет» (I am 20); «Мне холодно» (I am cold); «Мне нужно работать» (I need to work). The word for «year» depends on the number: «год» with 1 (21 год), «года» with 2, 3 and 4 (22 года), «лет» with 5 to 20 and with 25, 30... (25 лет). From 11 to 14 it is always «лет». Question: «Сколько тебе лет?»

Нам весело. Мне скучно. Ей страшно.
Мне нужно идти. Тебе надо отдыхать.

topicos.titulo: The instrumental: the "extension of the body"
topicos.explicacao: Picture a scene you will probably live. You are in Russia and you want to say that you write with a pen. You think: "pen in Russian is ру́чка, and 'with' is с, so I will say я пишу́ с ру́чкой." The person gives you a puzzled look and corrects you: — Я пишу́ ру́чкой. You stare. It is the same word, ру́чка, but now it is in the instrumental (ру́чкой) and you did not use с. You wonder: "But I wanted to say with the pen! Why no с?" And the person explains: — Because the pen does not go along with you. The pen is part of you when you write. The pen is the extension of your hand. That is the doorway into the instrumental case, and it shows a beauty that English hides. Pay attention: after this lesson you will understand one of the biggest differences between the two languages. The little secret: the extension of the body. In English, the word "with" has two completely different senses that we never notice. Sense 1, instrument (the thing is an extension of your body): I write with a pen. I eat soup with a spoon. I cut bread with a knife. I paint with a brush. Sense 2, company (the thing is another person, not an extension): I go with you. I live with my mother. I talk with the teacher. I work with my colleagues. English uses the same word "with" for both, automatically. Nobody thinks about it. In Russian this is impossible: the two "with" are different structures. Sense 1 (instrument) = the bare instrumental, with no preposition. Sense 2 (company) = С + instrumental. See for yourself. Notice: in the first case the pen and the spoon are extensions of the body. You write, and the pen is part of the movement of your hand. You eat, and the spoon is part of the movement of your hand. The thing does not go with you; at that moment it is you. In the second case you and the other person are two separate beings. You go, and they go. You live, and they live. That is company, so it needs с.

tabelas.titulo: The little secret: the extension of the body

linhas.ENGLISH: I eat soup with a spoon.

topicos.explicacao: The painter metaphor. Here is a metaphor worth the whole lesson. Imagine Da Vinci without a brush. How would he paint the Mona Lisa? He would not. The brush is an extension of his hand. Without it his hand cannot do the action of painting. The brush is part of Da Vinci at the moment of painting. In Russian, Da Vinci painted ки́стью (a brush: bare instrumental), not с ки́стью, because the brush was not a companion. It was an extension of his hand. Another example: you eat soup. Without a spoon you cannot eat soup (unless you lift the bowl, but that is another matter). The spoon is the extension of your hand at the moment of eating. So in Russian you eat soup ло́жкой (bare instrumental), not с ло́жкой. Third example: you write a letter. Without a pen you cannot write. The pen is the extension of your hand at the moment of writing. So you write ру́чкой, not с ру́чкой. Now compare with company: you go to the cinema. You go, and your friend goes. Your friend is not an extension of your body. Your friend is another person, with their own will, their own feet, their own path. So you go с дру́гом (with the friend: С + instrumental). That is all. The rule is one question: is the thing an extension of your body? YES = bare instrumental (ру́чкой, ло́жкой, ки́стью). NO (it is another person or an independent thing) = С + instrumental (с дру́гом, с ма́мой). The magic question solves about 90% of cases. Here is how you decide between the bare instrumental and С + instrumental.

tabelas.titulo: The magic question: is the thing an extension of the body?

linhas.SENTENCE: I eat soup with a spoon.
I cut bread with a knife.

topicos.explicacao: The 6 prepositions of the instrumental. Besides «с» (company), the instrumental is governed by 6 main prepositions. All of them express an idea of position or relation. One big rule: the change always comes AFTER the preposition. The preposition itself never changes; it is fixed. What changes is the word that follows it: the noun goes into the instrumental. Look at the examples. Notice that the preposition (над, под, пе́ред, ме́жду, за, с) is always the same, and it is the noun that takes the instrumental ending. That is why we say the preposition "governs" the instrumental: it demands that the word after it be in that case.

linhas.EXAMPLE: пе́ред до́мом (in front of the house)
ме́жду столо́м и дива́ном (between the table and the sofa)

linhas.PREPOSITION + NOUN: ме́жду + стол и диван → ме́жду столо́м и дива́ном
linhas.WHAT CHANGED: стол became столо́м, диван became дива́ном

topicos.explicacao: The instrumental answers «кем? чем?». In English we use "with" and "by means of". Singular: hard masculine: -ом (брат → братом); soft masculine (-й, -ь): -ем (учитель → учителем, музей → музеем). After ж, ч, ш, щ and ц: -ем if the ending is unstressed (муж → мужем) and -ом if it is stressed (врач → врачом). Feminine: -а → -ой (мама → мамой); -я → -ей (неделя → неделей); -ь → -ью (ночь → ночью, дочь → дочерью). Neuter: -о → -ом (окно → окном); -е → -ем (море → морем). Plural, all genders: -ами or -ями (книги → книгами, студенты → студентами). Irregular: друзья → друзьями, дети → детьми, люди → людьми.
topicos.comparacao: in English "with my brother" does not change the word "brother". In Russian the noun itself changes: «с братом».

erros.motivo: The pronoun goes into the instrumental: с ним.

tabelas.titulo: Pronouns (after «с» the 3rd person gets an н-)

topicos.titulo: The crucial distinction: place (instrumental) vs. movement (accusative)
topicos.explicacao: The crucial distinction: place (instrumental) vs. movement (accusative). Here is a trap that catches almost every learner. The prepositions ПОД and ЗА change case according to the meaning: Place (rest) = instrumental. Movement = accusative. Look. The rule: place (where it is) = instrumental; movement (where it goes) = accusative. English hides this because "under the table" is the same whether the cat is lying there or running there. It is the same logic you already saw with В and НА in lesson 16 (where = prepositional; where to = accusative). Here: where = instrumental; where to = accusative. Two prepositions in this group never change: НАД (above) and ПЕ́РЕД (in front of) always take the instrumental, and МЕ́ЖДУ (between) normally does too. So the trap is really about ПОД and ЗА. Compare with В and НА (lesson 16). Notice: the accusative is always the case of movement. The case of rest changes: prepositional with В/НА, instrumental with ПОД/ЗА.

tabelas.titulo: The crucial distinction: place (instrumental) vs. movement (accusative)

linhas.SENTENCE: The cat is under the table.
The cat runs under the table.
The picture is above the table.
He puts the box under the table.
The house is behind the garden.

topicos.titulo: Endings and master table of the instrumental
topicos.explicacao: The instrumental method. Now the endings. The method is the same as always: STEP 1: find the nominative form (the dictionary form). STEP 2: add the instrumental ending, which depends on the gender. STEP 3: done, the noun is in the instrumental. Notice: masculine and neuter get -ОМ/-ЕМ. Feminine in -а/-я gets -ОЙ/-ЕЙ (or the older, poetic -ОЮ/-ЕЮ). Feminine in -ь gets -ЬЮ. Neuter in -мя gets -ЕНЕМ. The big difference from the other cases: masculine and neuter both get -ОМ/-ЕМ (not -У, not -Е). It is a single ending. Then comes the master table of the instrumental. Watch the spelling rule: after the letters ж, ч, ш, щ, ц, an unstressed -ОМ/-ОЙ is written -ЕМ/-ЕЙ: това́рищ → това́рищем (not "това́рищом"); врач → врачо́м (stressed, so it stays -ом); муж → му́жем (not "мужом"); ноша → но́шей.

tabelas.titulo: The master table of the instrumental

topicos.titulo: The preposition с/со and the pronouns in the instrumental
topicos.explicacao: The С / СО variation. The preposition с (with) has a spelling variant. С is used before most words: с дру́гом, с ма́мой, с учи́телем. СО is used before words that begin with a hard-to-say cluster of consonants (for example с, ш, ж or в followed by another consonant) and before мн-, and it is also used in the very common со мной (with me): со мной, со стака́ном, со всеми́. Why? Ease of pronunciation again. «С дру́гом» is easy to say. But stacking several consonants in a row (с + мн, с + вс) would be a mouthful, so Russian inserts an -о- as a cushion: со мной. English does something similar with "a" and "an". The personal pronouns in the instrumental. As in the dative, the personal pronouns have special instrumental forms, and you have to learn them. Watch the rule of the "н": when он, она́, оно́, они́ come after a preposition, they get an н- at the start: с ним (with him), с ней (with her), с ни́ми (with them), о нём (about him: prepositional), к нему́ (to him: dative). But when the pronoun does not follow a preposition, there is no н: его́ (his / him, with no preposition), её (her), их (their / them).

linhas.TRANSLATION: off the table (this is the genitive, a different use of со)
I love him. (no preposition, so no н-)

topicos.explicacao: Five main uses. (1) Company, with «с»: «с другом». (2) Instrument or means, WITHOUT a preposition: «писать ручкой», «есть ложкой». (3) Profession with «работать» and «быть»: «Я работаю врачом», «Он хочет быть учителем». (4) Time: «утром, днём, вечером, ночью» and the seasons «зимой, весной, летом, осенью». (5) Place, with the prepositions «над» (above), «под» (under), «перед» (in front of), «за» (behind) and «между» (between), and also «рядом с» (next to): «Лампа стоит над столом».

erros.motivo: After «работать», the profession goes into the instrumental.

linhas.exemplo: Я пишу ручкой. Я ем вилкой.
Зимой я читаю. Вечером я дома.

topicos.titulo: Support tables and verbs with the instrumental
topicos.explicacao: Support tables: plural, adjectives and possessives in the instrumental. Verbs that take the instrumental. Some verbs always take the instrumental. Here are the main ones. Watch the verb быть: in the past and the future it usually takes the instrumental for what someone is. This is one of the most important rules. Notice: быть in the past or future puts the predicate (what the person is) in the instrumental. But быть does not exist in the present (you know that from Lesson 4), so in the present the predicate stays in the nominative: Я студе́нт. (I am a student: no verb, nominative.) Я был студе́нтом. (I was a student: with the verb, instrumental.) English has no case here at all, so the thing to memorise is simply the pattern: was / will be / became + instrumental.

topicos.explicacao: The idiom мы с X. This is one of the most elegant constructions in Russian. When Russian wants to say "X and I", it says "we with X". How to use it: the subject is always мы (we), even when the group is only two people, and the verb is plural. The «с» + instrumental names the other person. Notice what English does: "Eva and I" lists two people with "and". Russian says "we, together with Eva". In place of "my husband and I", Russian says "we with the husband". It is used all the time in daily life.

linhas.RUSSIAN: Мы с Е́вой реши́ли пое́хать в Сиби́рь.
linhas.TRANSLATION: Eva and I decided to go to Siberia.

linhas.RUSSIAN: Мы с му́жем живём в Москве́.
linhas.TRANSLATION: My husband and I live in Moscow.

linhas.RUSSIAN: Мы с дру́гом идём в кино́.
linhas.TRANSLATION: My friend and I are going to the cinema.

topicos.explicacao: The instrumental of time. Some time expressions use the instrumental with no preposition. You have seen this in passing with the prepositional; this is the right place for it. Notice that these adverbs are really instrumental forms of nouns (у́тро → у́тром, день → днём, ве́чер → ве́чером, ночь → но́чью). That is why they count as instrumental. But you do not need to think about that, you only need to use them. English does the same job with "in the" or with no word at all ("mornings", "in summer").

linhas.TRANSLATION: In the morning I drink coffee.

topicos.titulo: Common mistakes, sentences and summary of the instrumental
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistakes English speakers WILL make with the instrumental. Mistake 1: using С when it is not needed. Wrong: Я пишу́ с ру́чкой. Right: Я пишу́ ру́чкой. You think "with a pen" and translate it as «с ручкой». But the pen is an extension of the hand, so there is no С: bare instrumental. Mistake 2: leaving out С when it is needed. Wrong: Я иду́ дру́гом. Right: Я иду́ с дру́гом. The friend is another person, not an extension of your body, so С is needed. Mistake 3: using С with tools. Wrong: Я ем суп с ло́жкой. Right: Я ем суп ло́жкой. The spoon is an extension of the hand: bare instrumental. Mistake 4: forgetting that ПОД and ЗА change case. Wrong: Кот под стол (meaning "the cat is under the table"). Right: Кот под столо́м. Place = instrumental. Movement = accusative. Mistake 5: forgetting the С / СО variation. Wrong: Он идёт с мной. Right: Он идёт со мной. Mistake 6: leaving out н- after a preposition. Wrong: Я иду́ с им. Right: Я иду́ с ним. After a preposition, он becomes ним (with н). Mistake 7: not using the instrumental with быть in the past or future. Wrong: Я был студе́нт. Right: Я был студе́нтом. Быть in the past usually puts the predicate in the instrumental. Mistake 8: mixing up быть in the present (nominative) with быть in the past (instrumental). Wrong: Я студе́нтом. (in the present) Right: Я студе́нт (nominative: present). Я был студе́нтом (instrumental: past). Быть does not exist in the present, so the predicate stays in the nominative; only in the past and the future does it go into the instrumental. Mistake 9: forgetting that МЕ́ЖДУ takes the instrumental. Wrong: Ме́жду стол и дива́н. Right: Ме́жду столо́м и дива́ном. Ме́жду takes the instrumental on both sides. Mistake 10: leaving the noun in the nominative where an instrument ending is needed. Wrong: Я пишу́ ру́чка. Right: Я пишу́ ру́чкой. Masculine and neuter: -ОМ/-ЕМ. Feminine in -а: -ОЙ. Feminine in -ь: -ЬЮ. STEP 2: Full sentences with the instrumental. Here are real sentences, so you can see the instrumental at work. STEP 3: Summary table: the instrumental case.

linhas.TRANSLATION: I eat soup with a spoon.
I cut bread with a knife.
The cat is under the table.
The lamp is above the table.
The house is behind the garden.
In front of the house there are trees.
Between the table and the sofa there is a lamp.

linhas.RUSSIAN: Мы с Е́вой идём в кино́.
linhas.TRANSLATION: Eva and I are going to the cinema.
In the morning I drink coffee.

topicos.explicacao: Picture a scene you will probably live. You are in Russia, in a shop, and you want to say that you have no money. You think: "money in Russian is де́ньги, so I will say у меня́ нет де́ньги." The person looks at you and corrects: — У меня́ нет де́нег. You stare. It is the same word, де́ньги, but now it is де́нег, with no -и at the end. You wonder: "Haven't I already changed this word once? Why did it change again? How many forms does it have?" This happens to every learner of Russian the first time they meet the genitive, and it is where many give up. Let me be honest: this is the most complex case in Russian. But in this lesson I will do two things. STEP 1: I will explain the genitive so clearly that it looks simple. STEP 2: I will split the genitive over two lessons so you do not quit halfway. This is lesson 27: the genitive as "of" and as negation. Only that: no plural, no numbers, no prepositions; those wait for lesson 28. And before we begin, some reassurance: you are finishing the tedious part of Russian. The essential grammar ends here. What comes next is not harder, it is richer. First, what does "genitive" mean? A little etymology helps. The word comes from Latin genitivus, a Latin version of a Greek term meaning the case of the "kind" or "family" something belongs to; it is related to genus, to gignere ("to beget") and to the words gene and genetics. So the genitive is the case of origin and belonging. When you say "Ivan's book", you are saying that the book belongs to Ivan, comes from Ivan, is tied to Ivan. Unlike many languages, English has two ways to do this: "of" (the book of the teacher, the centre of the city, the colour of the sea) and the ending 's (Ivan's book, my mother's house). Look: in all these phrases the "of" or the 's shows possession, belonging or origin. That is what the genitive does in Russian. It is the case of "of" and of 's. And genetics is a nice memory hook: the genitive is the "genetic case" of the sentence, the case that marks whom a thing comes from.

topicos.titulo: Genitive singular: the "of" and the endings
topicos.explicacao: A bridge with English. Before any table, let us build the bridge. English expresses the genitive in two ways. Way 1, with "of": the book of Ivan. The house of my mother. Way 2, with 's: Ivan's book. My mother's house. In Russian, this is where the two meet: there is no separate word "of" and no 's. What exists is a change in the ending of the noun. Кни́га Ива́на is literally "book Ivan-of" (Ivan with the genitive ending). That is why the case is called the genitive: it marks origin, possession, belonging, with no word "of", only with an ending. The endings of the genitive singular. Now the endings. The method is the same as always: STEP 1: find the nominative form (the dictionary form). STEP 2: add the genitive ending, which depends on the gender and on the ending of the word. STEP 3: done, the noun is in the genitive. Notice: masculine and neuter take -А/-Я. Feminine takes -Ы/-И (or -ИИ after -ия). Neuter in -мя takes -ЕНИ. That is all. Let us see each case in detail.

linhas.ENGLISH: The house of my mother. (My mother's house.)
The name of the boy. (The boy's name.)

linhas.GENITIVE SINGULAR: -Ы (or -И after г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ)

topicos.explicacao: The MASCULINE in the genitive. Masculine in a consonant → -А. Notice: the -А is added at the end of the word. Masculine in -й → -Я. Notice: the -й disappears and -Я comes in. Masculine in -ь → -Я. Notice: the -ь disappears and -Я comes in. Watch the stress: слова́рь → словаря́ (stress on the ending), but учи́тель → учи́теля (stress on the stem). There is no fixed rule. You have to listen and memorise.

tabelas.titulo: The MASCULINE in the genitive: consonant → -А

topicos.explicacao: The genitive answers «кого? чего?» (of whom? of what?). It is the most used case in Russian. Singular (seen already): -а → -ы; -я → -и; consonant → -а; masculine -й and -ь → -я; -о → -а; -е → -я; feminine -ь → -и. After г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ write -и. Plural: masculine: consonant → -ов (стол → столов); -й → -ев (музей → музеев); -ь, ж, ч, ш, щ → -ей (словарь → словарей, врач → врачей). Feminine and neuter: the ending disappears (zero): книга → книг, окно → окон. But -я → -ь (неделя → недель) and -ие → -ий. Sometimes a fleeting vowel appears: сестра → сестёр, девушка → девушек. Irregular: друзья → друзей, дети → детей, люди → людей, семья → семей.
topicos.comparacao: English uses «of» for almost everything («the brother's book», «without books»). In Russian the word changes its ending instead of getting an «of».

topicos.explicacao: The FEMININE in the genitive. Feminine in -а → -Ы (or -И after г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ). Watch the letters г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ: after them the ending is -И (not -Ы). This is a Russian spelling rule. Feminine in -я → -И. Notice: the -я disappears and -И comes in. Feminine in -ь → -И. Notice: the -ь disappears and -И comes in. Feminine in -ия → -ИИ. Notice: the -я disappears and -ИИ comes in (two "i"s).

tabelas.titulo: After г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ → -И

topicos.titulo: Neuter and the master table of the genitive singular
topicos.explicacao: The NEUTER in the genitive. Neuter in -о → -А. Notice: the -о becomes -А. Neuter in -е → -Я. Notice: the -е becomes -Я. Neuter in -мя → -ЕНИ. Notice: there are about 10 such words, and you have known them since lesson 11. They are neuter and end in -мя. In the genitive they become -мени. The master table of the genitive singular solves everything. The big difference to remember: masculine and neuter take -А/-Я; feminine takes -Ы/-И.

У меня́ нет э́той но́вой кни́ги.

topicos.titulo: The first use: NEGATION ("I don't have")
topicos.explicacao: The first use: NEGATION ("I don't have"). Now that you know the endings, here is the first practical use, and it is good news: the negation of possession is the gateway to the genitive. It is the easiest and most frequent use. You already know from lesson 6 how to say "I have": У меня́ есть кни́га. (I have a book.) To say "I don't have a book", Russian swaps есть for нет and puts the object in the genitive: У меня́ нет кни́ги. (I have no book.) Notice: кни́га became кни́ги. That is the genitive singular. Compare. The logic is simple: Есть (have) + nominative. Нет (don't have) + genitive. Why the genitive? Here is a handy way to picture it: if I have a book, the book is mine, it belongs to me. If I don't have it, nothing belongs to me, and the genitive, the case of belonging, marks that missing belonging. English has a faint hint of this idea in "I have no book", where "no" works like "not any" and you are left with the empty set. Full sentences with "I don't have". Notice: all the objects are in the genitive, every one of them. It is a fixed rule: нет always takes the genitive. Careful: some of these sentences have a genitive plural (друзе́й, дете́й, де́нег). That belongs to lesson 28. For now focus on the genitive singular; the singular sentences are the easiest.

tabelas.titulo: The first use: NEGATION ("I don't have")

topicos.explicacao: Six uses. (1) Absence, with «нет»: «У меня нет времени». (2) Quantity: «много, мало, несколько, сколько, достаточно» + genitive plural for countable things (много книг) and genitive singular for what cannot be counted (много воды). (3) Measures and containers: «килограмм хлеба, литр молока, бутылка воды, чашка чая, кусок сыра». (4) Owner: «книга брата». (5) Prepositions: у, из, от, до, после, для, без, около, вокруг. (6) Origin and exit: «из» and «с» + genitive answer «откуда?» (where from?) and are the opposite of «в» and «на»: в школу → из школы; на работу → с работы.

erros.motivo: With «много» and countable things use the genitive plural.

linhas.exemplo: бутылка воды, чашка чая, кусок сыра

topicos.titulo: The second use: POSSESSION ("the book of...")
topicos.explicacao: The second use of the genitive is possession. It is the English "of" or 's. Compare. Notice: in Russian the first noun (the thing owned) stays in the nominative. The second noun (the owner) goes into the genitive. The "of" is not a separate word; it is the ending of the second noun. Structure: [thing owned, nominative] + [owner, genitive]. Examples in full sentences. Notice: the first noun (кни́га, дом, и́мя, центр, цвет, му́зыка, кры́ша, дверь) stays in the nominative. The second noun (Ива́на, ма́мы, ма́льчика, го́рода, мо́ря, компози́тора, до́ма, ко́мнаты) goes into the genitive. It is the owner. The magic question is "whose is it?" and the answer goes into the genitive. "Whose book? Ivan's." → Ива́на. Careful with the order: English can say "Ivan's book" (owner first), but Russian always puts the thing first and the owner after it, like English "the book of Ivan".

tabelas.titulo: The second use: POSSESSION ("the book of...")

linhas.TRANSLATION: This is the colour of the sea.
This is the roof of the house.
This is the door of the room.

topicos.titulo: The genitive with "нет" in sentences without у меня
topicos.explicacao: The word нет can also be used without у меня. It then means "there is not", "there is no". Notice: the object still goes into the genitive. Нет always takes the genitive, whether or not there is a «у меня». In context:

The mistakes English speakers WILL make with the genitive. Mistake 1: using the nominative instead of the genitive after «нет». Wrong: У меня́ нет кни́га. Right: У меня́ нет кни́ги. Нет always takes the genitive, without exception. Mistake 2: forgetting that feminine -а becomes -ы (or -и after г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ). Wrong: У меня́ нет кни́гы. Right: У меня́ нет кни́ги. (кни́га has a г before the -а, so it is -и.) Mistake 3: forgetting that feminine -я becomes -и. Wrong: У меня́ нет семья́. Right: У меня́ нет семьи́. Mistake 4: forgetting that feminine -ь becomes -и. Wrong: У меня́ нет дверь. Right: У меня́ нет две́ри. Mistake 5: forgetting that -ия becomes -ии. Wrong: Э́то центр Росси́е. Right: Э́то центр Росси́и (-ия always becomes -ии). Mistake 6: forgetting that -мя becomes -мени. Wrong: У меня́ нет вре́мя. Right: У меня́ нет вре́мени. Mistake 7: confusing the genitive with the animate accusative. For masculine animate nouns the genitive and the accusative have the same form (-а/-я), so it is easy to mix them up. But the function differs. Accusative: the object of the action. Я ви́жу дру́га. (I see my friend.) Genitive: possession or negation. У меня́ нет дру́га. (I have no friend.) The form is the same but the context is different. Don't worry about telling them apart for now; just know that after нет it is always genitive. Mistake 8: putting the thing owned in the genitive instead of the owner. Wrong: Ива́н кни́га (meaning "Ivan's book"). Right: Кни́га Ива́на. The thing owned (кни́га) stays in the nominative. The owner (Ива́н) goes into the genitive (Ива́на). Mistake 9: thinking every English "of" becomes a genitive. English "of" has many senses: possession ("the book of Ivan"), origin ("I am from Chicago"), material ("a table of wood"), subject ("we speak of music"). In Russian each sense has its own structure. The genitive covers possession and some origins. But "a wooden table" is an adjective (деревя́нный стол), not a genitive. For now, focus on the genitive of possession. Mistake 10: getting the stress wrong. Some words move their stress in the genitive: окно́ → окна́ (the stress moves), вода́ → воды́ (the stress moves), рука́ → руки́ (the stress moves). There is no fixed rule. You have to listen and memorise.

Before closing this lesson, a pause. Listen to what I am about to say. You are finishing the tedious part of Russian. The essential grammar ends here. You have already learned: the alphabet. The gender of nouns. The gender of adjectives. Verbs in the present, past and future. The nominative, accusative, prepositional, dative and instrumental cases. And now the first half of the genitive. Only one thing is missing: the second half of the genitive (plural, numbers, prepositions). We do that in lesson 28. After that you will have all 6 cases of Russian. What comes next is not harder, it is richer: vocabulary, expressions, culture, immersion. You will be able to read, write, listen and speak Russian at A1/A2 level. The learner's mistake is to think the advanced stage is the hard one. In Russian the hard part is the basic structure, because it is abstract, full of rules and full of exceptions. Once you master the structure, everything else flows. You already have the structure. One lesson left, in two parts. And after that, Russian will be yours. а → ы (г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ → и) · я, ь → и

topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: • 1. The genitive is the case of origin and belonging (the name is tied to Latin genitivus and to words like genus and genetics). It marks who something belongs to. STEP 2: • 2. The genitive corresponds to the English "of" and 's: the book of Ivan, Mum's house. STEP 3: • 3. Genitive singular endings: STEP 4: Masculine in a consonant: -А (друг → дру́га) STEP 5: Masculine in -й/-ь: -Я (учи́тель → учи́теля) STEP 6: Feminine in -а: -Ы (кни́га → кни́ги; after г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ → -И) STEP 7: Feminine in -я/-ь: -И (семья́ → семьи́, ночь → но́чи) STEP 8: Feminine in -ия: -ИИ (Росси́я → Росси́и) STEP 9: Neuter in -о: -А (окно́ → окна́) STEP 10: Neuter in -е: -Я (мо́ре → мо́ря) STEP 11: Neuter in -мя: -ЕНИ (вре́мя → вре́мени) STEP 12: • 4. First use: NEGATION. STEP 13: Есть (have) + nominative: У меня́ есть кни́га. STEP 14: Нет (don't have) + genitive: У меня́ нет кни́ги. STEP 15: • 5. Second use: POSSESSION. STEP 16: Thing owned (nominative) + owner (genitive): Кни́га Ива́на. STEP 17: • 6. Нет always takes the genitive. Always. No exceptions. STEP 18: • 7. Typical learner mistakes: using the nominative after нет; forgetting -и after г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ; forgetting -мя → -мени; confusing the genitive with the animate accusative; putting the thing owned in the genitive.

Where you are now. In lesson 27 you learned the genitive singular, the "of" and the negation. You can already say: У меня́ нет кни́ги. (I have no book.) Э́то дом ма́мы. (It is Mum's house.) У меня́ нет вре́мени. (I have no time.) Now the second half. In this lesson you will learn: STEP 1: the genitive plural, how to say "I have no books" (нет книг). STEP 2: numbers, how to say "two books" (две кни́ги) and "five books" (пять книг). STEP 3: the prepositions of the genitive: без, для, до, из, от, у. After this lesson you will have finished the essential grammar of Russian, because you will have seen all 6 cases. I explain that at the end. The genitive plural works like the singular, but with different endings. English plurals just add -s; Russian plural endings depend on the gender and the last letter, and in the genitive plural many feminine and neuter nouns lose their ending completely. Here are the main rules, and I will go through each case with examples.

linhas.GENDER / ENDING: Masculine in ж, ч, ш, щ

topicos.titulo: The masculine in the genitive plural
topicos.explicacao: The masculine in the genitive plural. Hard masculine → -ОВ. Notice: you add -ОВ to the end of the word. It is the most common masculine rule. Watch the irregulars: друг → друзе́й (not "другов"). Брат → бра́тьев (not "братов"). These are exceptions you will learn by heart. Soft masculine (-ь, -й) → -ЕЙ (and -ЕВ after -й). Notice: the -ь or -й disappears and -ЕЙ comes in. Masculine in ж, ч, ш, щ → -ЕЙ. Notice: after ж, ч, ш, щ the ending is -ЕЙ (not -ОВ).

tabelas.titulo: The masculine in the genitive plural: hard
The masculine in the genitive plural: soft
The masculine in the genitive plural: ж, ч, ш, щ

topicos.titulo: The feminine in the genitive plural
topicos.explicacao: The feminine in the genitive plural. Feminine in -а → no ending. Notice: the -а disappears and the word is just the stem, with no ending at all. This is the most frequent feminine plural, but it is not always so simple; see the next topic on the fleeting vowel. Feminine in -я → -Ь. Notice: the -я disappears and -Ь (the soft sign) comes in, or a fleeting vowel appears. Feminine in -ь → -ЕЙ. Notice: the -ь disappears and -ЕЙ comes in. Feminine in -ия → -ИЙ. Notice: the -я disappears and -ИЙ comes in (with two "i"s, one of them the letter й).

topicos.titulo: The neuter in the genitive plural
topicos.explicacao: The neuter in the genitive plural. Neuter in -о → no ending. Notice: the -о disappears. Sometimes a fleeting vowel appears (о́кон, пи́сем; see the next topic). Neuter in -е → -ЕЙ. Notice: the -е disappears and -ЕЙ comes in (words in -ие take -ИЙ instead: упражне́ний). Neuter in -мя → -ЁН. Notice: these 10 or so words are neuter and end in -мя. In the genitive plural they become -ЁН (with a stressed ё).

topicos.titulo: The fleeting vowel: the secret of the feminine and neuter plural
topicos.explicacao: The fleeting vowel: the secret of the feminine and neuter plural. This is one of the rules that confuse learners most, yet it is predictable once you see the logic. When the stem ends in two consonants, a vowel (о or е) is inserted between them in the genitive plural to make the word easier to say. The logic: Russian dislikes hard consonant clusters at the end of a word, so it adds a vowel. English does the same thing when it says "film" as "fil-um" or "athlete" as "ath-a-lete". Examples with о and with е follow below. A practical rule: before the last consonant, after ж, ч, ш, щ (and after ь or й) you usually get -ЕК (кошек, девочек); after other consonants you usually get -ОК (палок, окон). Careful: there are exceptions. If in doubt, check a dictionary. The most common words you will end up memorising. Examples in sentences:

topicos.explicacao: Russian numerals are built by adding, from the biggest part to the smallest: 21 = двадцать один; 35 = тридцать пять; 148 = сто сорок восемь. From 13 to 19 you add -надцать to the base (тринадцать). The tens from 50 to 80 have a -ь- in the middle: пятьдесят, шестьдесят, семьдесят, восемьдесят. Watch 40 (сорок) and 90 (девяносто), which are special. Hundreds: сто, двести, триста, четыреста, пятьсот, шестьсот, семьсот, восемьсот, девятьсот.

The most common irregular plurals. Some words have an irregular genitive plural, and you have to memorise the main ones. Notice: some end in -ЬЕВ (братьев, деревьев, перьев, крыльев), others in -ЕЙ (друзей, мужей, детей, людей), and others have no ending (яблок, денег, суток). Keep these, because they come up all the time in daily life. English has irregular plurals too (man/men, child/children, foot/feet), so this is the same kind of memory work.

The big application: NUMBERS. Now we reach the most practical part of the genitive plural, and one of the most famous rules in Russian. The number 1 goes with the nominative singular. The numbers 2, 3 and 4 go with the genitive singular. The numbers 5 and up go with the genitive plural. English only has "one book" and "two or more books"; Russian has three groups. Let us see it with the word "book" (кни́га). Notice: the genitive singular is used with 2, 3, 4, and the genitive plural with 5+. Then with "table" (стол) and with "window" (окно́). Notice: the pattern is always the same. 1 → nominative singular. 2-4 → genitive singular. 5+ → genitive plural. The "last number" rule: when the number is compound, the last number decides. That is why Russian is logical: the last number of the sequence decides. Examples in sentences follow. The forms of "1" and "2" for each gender. The number 1 and the number 2: notice that the number 2 has два (masculine/neuter) and две (feminine). That is an important distinction. The numbers 3 and 4 do not change with gender: три, четы́ре.

The prepositions of the genitive. Now the prepositions that take the genitive. These are the most important. I will explain each with examples. БЕЗ: without. Notice: the object after без goes into the genitive. ДЛЯ: for. Notice: the object after для goes into the genitive. ДО: until, before. ИЗ: from (origin). Notice: из shows origin, where something comes out of. Do not confuse it with от, which shows moving away from a person. ОТ: from (moving away). Notice: от is used with people (moving away from them). Из is used with places (origin). У: at, by, at someone's place. Notice: у is already familiar from the "have" sentences (у меня́ есть). Here it means "by" or "at someone's place". О́КОЛО: near. КРО́МЕ: except. ПО́СЛЕ: after.

linhas.TRANSLATION: as far as work, before work

topicos.explicacao: The noun changes with the number. After 1 (and 21, 31...): nominative singular: один студент, двадцать одна книга. After 2, 3 and 4 (and 22, 23, 24...): genitive singular: два студента, три книги, четыре окна. After 5 to 20 and after 25, 30...: genitive plural: пять студентов, десять книг, двадцать окон. The numerals 1 and 2 have gender: один / одна / одно; два / две (feminine). Age: «год» with 1 (21 год), «года» with 2 to 4 (22 года), «лет» with 5 and up (25 лет); from 11 to 14 it is always «лет».
topicos.comparacao: English only switches to the plural from 2 on, and only has two forms ("one book", "two books"). Russian has three rules: 1, 2 to 4, and 5 and up.

topicos.titulo: Quantity and support tables for the genitive plural
topicos.explicacao: The big application: QUANTITY. Certain words of quantity take the genitive. The most important are in the table below. Notice: all of them take the genitive, always. Examples in sentences follow. The rule: мно́го, ма́ло, немно́го, ско́лько, сто́лько and не́сколько always take the genitive. And is it the genitive singular or plural? It depends on the word. Uncountable words (са́хар, вода́, вре́мя) → genitive singular (мно́го са́хара, ма́ло вре́мени). Countable words (кни́га, стол, дом) → genitive plural (мно́го книг, ма́ло столо́в). It is the same split English makes between "much" and "many": if the thing is countable, plural; if uncountable, singular. topicos.titulo: Common mistakes and sentences in the genitive plural
topicos.explicacao: The mistakes English speakers WILL make with the genitive plural. Mistake 1: using the singular after «нет» when the thing is plural. Wrong: У меня́ нет кни́ги. (singular, but you meant several books) Right: У меня́ нет книг. (plural) You learned the genitive singular in lesson 27 and tend to use it everywhere. But when the thing is plural, the genitive is plural. Mistake 2: adding -ОВ to a feminine in -а (instead of dropping the ending). Wrong: У меня́ нет ма́мов / кни́гов. Right: У меня́ нет мам / книг. Mistake 3: forgetting the -ОВ on a hard masculine. Wrong: У меня́ нет стол. Right: У меня́ нет столо́в. A hard masculine takes -ОВ. Mistake 4: using -ОВ on soft or sibilant stems that need -ЕЙ. Wrong: У меня́ нет учи́телов / врачо́в. Right: У меня́ нет учителе́й / враче́й. Mistake 5: forgetting the fleeting vowel. Wrong: У меня́ нет ко́шк. Right: У меня́ нет ко́шек. The fleeting vowel is obligatory when the stem ends in two consonants. Mistake 6: mixing up the number rules. Wrong: У меня́ пять кни́ги. Right: У меня́ пять книг. 5+ takes the genitive PLURAL, not the singular. It is one of the most confused rules. Mistake 7: forgetting that 2, 3, 4 take the genitive SINGULAR. Wrong: У меня́ две книг. Right: У меня́ две кни́ги. 2, 3, 4 take the genitive SINGULAR, not the plural. It is the opposite of the previous mistake. Mistake 8: forgetting that 1 goes with the nominative. Wrong: У меня́ одна́ кни́ги. Right: У меня́ одна́ кни́га. 1 goes with the nominative singular. It is the only number that does not take the genitive. Mistake 9: using the wrong gender with the number 2. Wrong: два кни́ги. Right: две кни́ги. Два is masculine/neuter. Две is feminine. Кни́га is feminine, so две. Mistake 10: forgetting the genitive after БЕЗ, ДЛЯ, ДО, ИЗ, ОТ, У. Wrong: без са́хар. Right: без са́хара. Wrong: для ма́ма. Right: для ма́мы. All the prepositions of the genitive take the genitive, always. Full sentences with the genitive plural. Here are real sentences.

topicos.titulo: Closing the essential grammar and summary of the genitive
topicos.explicacao: A final word of reassurance: you have finished the essential grammar. Now a pause. Listen to what I am about to say. You have finished the essential grammar of Russian. You have now seen all 6 cases: STEP 1: Nominative, the case of the subject. STEP 2: Accusative, the case of the action. STEP 3: Prepositional, the case of place. STEP 4: Dative, the case of things that happen to you. STEP 5: Instrumental, the case of the extensions of the body and of "with". STEP 6: Genitive, the case of possession, origin and negation. You already know the alphabet. The gender of nouns. The gender of adjectives. Verbs in the present, past and future. Personal pronouns, possessives and demonstratives. Numbers. The main prepositions. And here is the truth nobody tells you: the hard part of Russian is over. The learner's mistake is to think the advanced stage is the hard one. In Russian the hard part is the basic structure, because it is abstract, full of rules and full of exceptions. You faced that part and you won. What comes next is not harder, it is richer. After the genitive, Russian opens up into vocabulary (thousands of new words), idioms (learning to talk like a Russian), culture (understanding why Russians say what they say) and immersion (reading books, listening to music, watching films, talking with Russians). All of that is much easier than grammar, because it is intuitive, cultural and alive. You already have the structure. Now you build the house. One thing is left: practice. Read, listen, speak, write, every day, even if only for 15 minutes, because structure only consolidates with use. Summary table: the genitive plural.

Ordinals are adjectives: they agree with the noun. Masculine: первый, второй, третий...; feminine: первая, вторая, третья...; neuter: первое, второе, третье.... «Третий» is special (третья, третье, третьи). To give the date, use the ordinal in the NEUTER and the month in the GENITIVE: «первое мая» (1 May, "the first of May"). To say "on" a date, the ordinal also goes into the genitive: «первого мая» (on 1 May). Uses: floor («на третьем этаже»), order («второй урок»).

My birthday is on the tenth of June.

topicos.aulaTitulo: The big picture of the cases
topicos.explicacao: This is the chart that organises everything: six cases × three genders × singular and plural. Read it by columns: each column (masculine, feminine, neuter, plural) has its own pattern. The golden rule of the accusative: if the noun is inanimate (a thing), the accusative equals the nominative in the masculine, the neuter and the plural; in the feminine, -а becomes -у. If it is animate (a person or an animal), the accusative equals the genitive in the masculine and in the plural. The prepositional always comes with a preposition (в, на, о, при) and in the plural it ends in -ах or -ях. Examples: стол (m), книга (f), окно (n).

topicos.titulo: The six cases: adjectives and possessives
topicos.explicacao: The adjective and the possessive change along with the noun and always agree with it in gender, number and case. A trick: the adjective endings resemble the question of the case («какой? какого? какому? каким? о каком?»). The accusative follows the same rule as the nouns: inanimate = nominative; animate masculine and animate plural = genitive. Prepositional: -ом / -ой / -ом / -ых. English adjectives never change ("a new book", "with a new book"), so this agreement is new.

exemplos.pt: I am reading a new book.
I am going with my friend.
I live in a big city.

erros.motivo: The adjective goes into the accusative too.
The possessive and the noun change together.

topicos.aulaTitulo: The big picture of the cases
topicos.titulo: Pronouns and prepositions with each case
topicos.explicacao: Personal pronouns change in the six cases; after a preposition, the 3rd-person ones gain an н-: «у него», «к ней», «с ними». Each preposition takes a fixed case (or two, depending on the question): remember the rule of the questions «где?» (staying) and «куда?» (moving). For "in, on, at" with movement: accusative; staying put: prepositional. English shows the same case idea only in a few pronouns (I / me / my), so use that as a hook.

linhas.preposicao: у, из, от, до, после, для, без, около, вокруг, с (off, from)
